relationship: close image of intoxication without wine
rationale: Ephraim's hired men are described as drunk without wine; the later warning likewise describes a hangover from neither strong drink nor wine. The repeated denial of an ordinary intoxicant links the images without identifying the two audiences.
source_text: Woe to the crown of insolence, Ephraim’s hired men; the flower fallen from glory on the summit of the fertile mountain, those drunk without wine!

target_units.text: Grow faint, lose your senses and suffer a hangover, neither from sikera nor from wine,

relationship: close portrayal of wrath through violent hail and water
rationale: Both depict the Lord's forceful intervention through falling hail and violent water. Isaiah 28 additionally describes the land being given rest by His hands; Isaiah 30 emphasizes His voice and arm.
source_text: Behold, the Lord’s wrath is strong and harsh, like falling hail with no covering, falling violently. Like a great mass of water dragging a country, He will give the land rest with His hands.

target_units.text: God will make His voice’s glory heard and show His arm’s wrath with fury, anger and consuming flame. He will strike violently with lightning, like water and hail falling together violently.

relationship: related humiliation pictured through a lost crown
rationale: Ephraim's insolent crown is trampled underfoot; the lament declares that the crown has fallen from the community's head because of sin. Both use the crown's degradation to express communal humiliation, with different actions and communities.
source_text: Underfoot will be trampled the crown of insolence, Ephraim’s hired men.

target_units.text: The crown fell from our head; woe indeed to us, for we sinned!

relationship: close figure of fortifications or glory as easily swallowed figs
rationale: Isaiah's fading glory is like an early fig someone wants to swallow before taking it in hand; Nahum depicts fortresses as fig trees whose fruit falls into the eater's mouth when shaken. Nahum does not call its figs early.
source_text: The flower fallen from the hope of glory, on the high mountain’s summit, will be like an early fig: whoever sees it will want to swallow it before taking it into his hand.

target_units.text: All your fortresses are fig trees having lookouts; if shaken, they will fall into the eater’s mouth.

relationship: related crown imagery joining the Lord and His restored people
rationale: Here the Lord becomes a glorious crown for His remaining people; Isaiah 62 calls the restored city a beautiful crown in the Lord's hand. The shared royal adornment image has deliberately different directions.
source_text: On that day the Lord Sabaoth will be the crown of hope, woven of glory, for My people who remain;

target_units.text: You will be a crown of beauty in the Lord’s hand and a royal diadem in your God’s hand.

relationship: related spiritual endowment for strength and judgment
rationale: The remaining people receive a spirit of judgment and strength; the shoot from Jesse receives God's Spirit of counsel and might and judges the lowly. The latter describes one ruler rather than identifying him with the group in this verse.
source_text: they will be left with a spirit of judgment, for judgment and strength, as He prevents destruction.

target_units.text: And the Spirit of God will rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness.
The spirit of the fear of God will fill him. He will not judge according to appearance, nor reprove according to report;
but he will judge the cause of the lowly, and reprove the lowly of the earth; and he will strike the earth with the word of his mouth, and with breath through his lips he will slay the ungodly.

relationship: contrast between priestly sobriety and drunken failure
rationale: Isaiah describes priests and prophets losing their senses through wine and strong drink. Leviticus forbids Aaron and his sons those drinks while serving and connects the rule with distinguishing holy from profane and teaching Israel.
source_text: For these have been led astray by wine and wandered because of sikera. Priest and prophet lost their senses because of wine, reeled from sikera’s intoxication and went astray. This is an apparition.

target_units.text: You shall drink no wine or strong drink, you and your sons with you, when you enter the Tent of Testimony, or when you approach the altar, so that you do not die: an everlasting statute throughout your generations,
to distinguish between the holy and the profane, and between the unclean and the clean.
And you shall instruct the sons of Israel in all the statutes which the Lord spoke unto them by the hand of Moses.

relationship: parallel judgment upon religious counsel corrupted by gain
rationale: A curse consumes counsel directed toward greed, following Isaiah's description of priests and prophets. Micah names paid priestly answers and prophecy for silver before announcing Jerusalem's devastation; the forms of gain and judgment remain distinct.
source_text: A curse will consume this counsel, for this counsel is for greed.

target_units.text: Her leaders judged with gifts, her priests answered for wages and her prophets divined for silver; yet they relied upon the Lord, saying, “Is not the Lord among us? Calamities will certainly not come upon us.”
Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will be like a fruit watcher’s hut, and the mountain of the house like a forest grove.

relationship: related milk imagery for recipients of instruction
rationale: Isaiah addresses the recipients of a message as people weaned from milk; Hebrews describes learners who still need milk rather than solid food. Both use infancy and feeding to describe an instructional audience, but their stated stages differ.
source_text: To whom did we announce evils, and to whom did we announce a message—you weaned from milk, torn from a breast?

target_units.text: For although by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you the first elements of God’s oracles; you have come to need milk and not solid food.
For everyone who partakes of milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant.
But solid food belongs to the mature, whose faculties have been trained by practice to distinguish both good and evil.

relationship: same-chapter repetition of the affliction-and-hope refrain
rationale: The refrain affliction upon affliction, hope upon hope, and yet a little returns as what the Lord's utterance will become for the people. The later verse supplies the falling, breaking and capture associated with the repeated words.
source_text: Expect affliction upon affliction, hope upon hope, yet a little, yet a little,

target_units.text: The utterance of the Lord God will become for them affliction upon affliction, hope upon hope, yet a little, yet a little, so that they go and fall backward, come into danger, be shattered and captured.

relationship: explicit scriptural use of speech through other tongues
rationale: Paul cites speech to this people through other tongues and other lips, followed by their refusal to listen, and uses it when discussing tongues as a sign. Isaiah supplies the other-tongue wording and continues with refusal to hear in the next verse.
source_text: because of contemptuous lips, through another tongue, for they will speak to this people,

target_units.text: In the law it is written, “Through people of other tongues and through the lips of others I will speak to this people, and even so they will not listen to Me,” says the Lord.
So tongues are a sign for unbelievers, not for believers, while prophecy is for believers, not for unbelievers.

relationship: related offer of rest to people in need
rationale: Isaiah's reported speech names rest for the hungry, but the people refuse to listen; Jesus invites those laboring and burdened to receive His rest. Isaiah's additional language about shattering is not attributed to Jesus' invitation.
source_text: saying to it, “This is the rest for the hungry, and this is the shattering.” But they did not want to listen.

target_units.text: Come to Me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take My yoke upon you, and learn from Me; for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.
For My yoke is easy, and My burden is light.”

relationship: close sequence of falling, breaking and capture
rationale: Both warnings join falling, being broken and being captured. Isaiah 28 connects this outcome with the repeated utterance of affliction and hope; Isaiah 8 places it after the stone-and-trap warning.
source_text: The utterance of the Lord God will become for them affliction upon affliction, hope upon hope, yet a little, yet a little, so that they go and fall backward, come into danger, be shattered and captured.

target_units.text: Therefore many among them will be powerless, fall and be broken; people who are secure will draw near and be captured.”

relationship: parallel summons for rulers to hear the Lord's word
rationale: Both directly command rulers to hear the Lord's word. Isaiah 28 identifies Jerusalem's rulers, while Isaiah 1 addresses its rulers as rulers of Sodom; the different descriptions are retained.
source_text: Therefore hear the Lord’s word, afflicted men and rulers of this people in Jerusalem:

target_units.text: Hear the Lord’s word, rulers of Sodom! Attend to God’s law, people of Gomorrah!

relationship: close warning against hope placed in falsehood
rationale: Both passages describe reliance on falsehood before announcing the failure of that security. Here the speakers claim shelter through a covenant with death and Hades; Isaiah 30 uses the sudden collapse of a wall.
source_text: Because you said, “We made a covenant with Hades and agreements with death; if a rushing storm passes, it will certainly not come upon us. We made falsehood our hope and will be sheltered by deceit,”

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord, Israel’s Holy One: “Because you disobeyed these words and hoped in falsehood, and because you grumbled and came to trust in this word,
therefore this sin will be for you like a wall falling immediately in a captured fortified city, whose fall is immediately at hand,

relationship: explicit quotation of Zion's precious cornerstone
rationale: First Peter quotes the laying of a chosen, precious cornerstone in Zion and the assurance that the believer will not be ashamed. Its surrounding passage applies the stone imagery to Christ and the community built around Him.
source_text: therefore thus says the Lord: “Behold, I will place in Zion’s foundations a costly, chosen, precious cornerstone, in her foundations, and whoever trusts in it will certainly not be ashamed.

target_units.text: For it stands in Scripture: “Look, I am laying in Zion a stone, a chosen, precious cornerstone, and the one who believes in Him will certainly not be put to shame.”

relationship: combined stone citation joining trust and stumbling
rationale: Romans preserves the stone placed in Zion and the believer's freedom from shame, while combining them with stumbling-stone language. This differs from the costly cornerstone description here and serves Paul's contrast between faith and reliance on works.
source_text: therefore thus says the Lord: “Behold, I will place in Zion’s foundations a costly, chosen, precious cornerstone, in her foundations, and whoever trusts in it will certainly not be ashamed.

target_units.text: Why? Because it was not from faith, but as though from works. They stumbled against the stone of stumbling,
just as it is written, “Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, and the one who believes in Him will not be put to shame.”

relationship: related storm judgment exposing false security
rationale: Isaiah warns those trusting deceit that the storm will not pass them by; Proverbs says the impious disappears when a storm passes while the righteous is saved. The shared storm image concerns the failure of ungodly security; Proverbs does not repeat Isaiah's weights metaphor.
source_text: I will make judgment a hope, and My mercy will be weights; those trusting deceit do so in vain, for a storm will certainly not pass you by—

target_units.text: When a storm passes by, the impious disappears, but the righteous turns aside and is saved for ever.

relationship: parallel overthrow of false protection by a destructive storm
rationale: Isaiah questions the covenant with death and declares that hope toward Hades will fail when the rushing storm makes its claimants a trampling ground. Ezekiel exposes false peace through a coated wall torn down by downpour and violent wind. The covenant and wall are different images of unreliable protection.
source_text: might it also remove your covenant with death? Your hope toward Hades will certainly not remain. If a rushing storm comes, you will become its trampling ground.

target_units.text: Because they misled My people, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace, and this one builds a wall, and they coat it—if it is going to fall,

say to those coating it, ‘It will fall.’ There will be a flooding downpour, and I will put stones for hurling into their bonds, and they will fall; there will be an upending wind, and it will be split.
And behold, the wall has fallen! Will they not say to you, ‘Where is your coating with which you coated it?’
Therefore thus says the Lord: I will unleash an upending blast with wrath; a flooding downpour will come in My anger, and I will bring the projectile stones in wrath for complete destruction,

and I will tear down the wall you coated, and it will fall. I will lay it upon the ground; its foundations will be uncovered, and it will fall, and you will be brought to an end with rebukes. You will recognize that I am the Lord.

relationship: related night-and-morning language joined to learning under judgment
rationale: Isaiah 28 describes the recurring storm by morning, day and night and commands people to learn to listen. Isaiah 26 names the Lord's way as judgment, speaks of seeking Him from night into early morning, and commands the earth's inhabitants to learn righteousness.
source_text: When it passes, it will take you; morning after morning it will pass during the day, and at night there will be evil hope. Learn to listen!

target_units.text: For the Lord’s way is judgment. We hoped in Thy name and in the remembrance
which our soul desires. From night my spirit rises early toward Thee, God, because Thine ordinances are light upon the earth. Learn righteousness, you dwelling upon the earth!

relationship: related divine intervention at Gabaon or Gibeon
rationale: Isaiah locates an extraordinary wrathful act in Gabaon's ravine; Joshua narrates the Lord's intervention, hail and defeat at Gibeon. Joshua separately names Aijalon's ravine, so the comparison does not equate every geographical detail.
source_text: Like a mountain of ungodly people he will rise and be in Gabaon’s ravine. With wrath he will do his deeds, a work of bitterness; his wrath will act strangely, and his bitterness is foreign.”

target_units.text: The Lord threw them into confusion before the sons of Israel, and the Lord crushed them with a great defeat at Gibeon. They pursued them along the ascent of Horonin and cut them down as far as Azekah and Makkedah.

As they fled before the sons of Israel down the descent of Horonin, the Lord hurled hailstones from heaven upon them as far as Azekah. More died from the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword in battle.

Then Joshua spoke to the Lord on the day God handed the Amorites over to Israel, when He crushed them at Gibeon and they were crushed before the sons of Israel. Joshua said, “Let the sun stand over Gibeon, and the moon over the ravine of Aijalon.”
The sun stood, and the moon remained still, until God repelled their enemies. The sun stood in the middle of heaven and did not advance toward sunset for a full day.
There was no such day before or afterward, when God listened to a human being, for the Lord fought alongside Israel.

relationship: close announcement of a completed and shortened judgment
rationale: Both passages announce a completed or shortened divine action across the earth or inhabited world. Isaiah 28 speaks of deeds and warns against stronger bonds; Isaiah 10 speaks of a word carried out in righteousness.
source_text: And you, do not rejoice, nor let your bonds grow stronger, because I heard from the Lord Sabaoth completed and shortened deeds, which He will do upon all the earth.

target_units.text: Even if Israel’s people becomes like the sea’s sand, their remnant will be saved; for He is completing and cutting short a word in righteousness,
because God will carry out a shortened word in the whole inhabited world.

relationship: close instructional summons to attend with the ear
rationale: Both speakers ask the hearer to attend to their words and give the ear to instruction. Isaiah introduces the farming illustration; Proverbs addresses a son and continues with keeping the words in the heart.
source_text: Give ear and hear my voice; pay attention and hear my words.

target_units.text: Son, attend to my utterance; apply your ear to my words,

relationship: related preparation of ground before sowing
rationale: Isaiah asks whether seed is prepared before the ground is worked; Jeremiah commands Judah to break up fallow ground and not sow among thorns. Both join preparing soil with sowing, while Jeremiah directs the agricultural image toward repentance.
source_text: Will the plowman plow all day? Or will he prepare seed before working the ground?

target_units.text: For thus says the Lord to the men of Judah and those dwelling in Jerusalem: Break up fallow ground for yourselves, and do not sow among thorns.

relationship: same-chapter answer concerning the sequence of cultivation
rationale: The preceding question concerns plowing and preparing seed; this verse describes leveling the surface and then sowing named crops. The connection is the question-and-answer movement within the agricultural illustration.
source_text: When he has leveled its surface, does he not then sow a little black cumin and cumin, and again sow wheat, barley and emmer within your borders?

target_units.text: Will the plowman plow all day? Or will he prepare seed before working the ground?

relationship: parallel blessing associated with divine instruction and discipline
rationale: Isaiah promises discipline through God's judgment and rejoicing; the psalm calls the person disciplined by the Lord and taught His law happy. The psalm adds relief from evil days, while Isaiah uses the surrounding cultivation illustration.
source_text: You will be disciplined by your God’s judgment and will rejoice.

target_units.text: Happy the person Thou disciplinest, Lord, whom Thou teachest from Thy law,
to soothe him from evil days, until a pit is dug for the sinner.

relationship: close assurance that divine anger will not last forever
rationale: Isaiah declares that God will not remain angry forever or trample with bitterness; the psalm likewise says He will not maintain wrath forever. The psalm does not repeat the bread and cultivation language surrounding Isaiah's promise.
source_text: will be eaten with bread. For I will not be angry with you for ever, nor will the sound of My bitterness trample you.

target_units.text: He will not be angry to the end, nor maintain wrath for ever.

relationship: historical counterpart to David's attack on Jerusalem
rationale: Ariel is named as the city against which David fought and is identified with Jerusalem later in the oracle. Second Samuel narrates David's attack on Jerusalem, capture of Zion and settlement there; it does not supply Isaiah's statement about eating with Moab.
source_text: Woe, city Ariel, against which David fought! Gather produce year after year, for you will eat with Moab.

target_units.text: David and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites inhabiting the land. David was told, “You will not come in here,” for the blind and the lame resisted, saying, “David will not come in here.”
David captured the stronghold of Zion, which is the city of David.

David said that day, “Everyone striking a Jebusite, let him attack with a dagger both the lame and the blind and those who hate David’s soul.” Therefore they will say, “The blind and the lame shall not enter the Lord’s house.”
David settled in the stronghold, and it was called the city of David. He built the city around from the citadel, and his own house.

relationship: parallel announcement of Jerusalem enclosed by siege works
rationale: Isaiah describes surrounding the city with a palisade and towers; Jesus warns Jerusalem of enemies building a siege barrier and hemming it in on every side. The shared siege pattern is explicit without identifying the two announcements as one event.
source_text: I will surround you like David, set a palisade around you and set towers around you,

target_units.text: For days will come upon you when your enemies will build a siege barrier around you and surround you and hem you in on every side.
They will dash you to the ground, and your children within you, and will not leave stone upon stone within you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.”

relationship: related imagery of a voice speaking from the earth
rationale: Jerusalem's humbled voice is compared with people who speak from the earth; Isaiah 8 names earth-speakers when warning against seeking the dead. The former is a comparison for humiliation, while the latter concerns an illicit practice.
source_text: and your words will be humbled into the earth and sink into the earth. Your voice will be like those who speak from the earth, and your voice will weaken toward the ground.

target_units.text: If they say to you, “Seek those who speak from the earth and the belly-speakers, the empty-talkers who speak from the belly,” should not a nation turn to its God? Why do they seek the dead concerning the living?

relationship: related chaff imagery for the ungodly and their wealth
rationale: Isaiah compares the wealth of the ungodly with drifting chaff and wheel-dust; the psalm compares the ungodly themselves with chaff flung away by wind. The shared dispersal image does not erase Isaiah's specific focus on wealth.
source_text: The wealth of the ungodly will be like dust from a wheel, like drifting chaff, and it will be like a moment, immediately,

target_units.text: Not so the ungodly, not so, but like chaff which the wind flings away from the face of the earth.

relationship: close depiction of divine visitation through storm and earthquake
rationale: Both portray divine intervention with earth shaking, thunder and fire, together with violent atmospheric imagery. Isaiah announces visitation amid the oracle about Ariel; the psalm describes the Lord's angry intervention in the speaker's deliverance.
source_text: from the Lord Sabaoth. For there will be a visitation with thunder, earthquake and a great sound, a rushing storm and a consuming flame of fire.

target_units.text: And the earth was shaken and began to tremble; the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken because God was angry with them.
Smoke rose in His anger, and fire from His face set things ablaze; coals were kindled from Him.
And He bent heaven and came down, and gloom was beneath His feet.
And He mounted cherubim and flew; He flew on the wings of winds.
And He made darkness His hiding place; His tent was around Him, dark water in clouds of the air.
From the far-shining radiance before Him, the clouds passed— hail and coals of fire.
And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave His voice.
And He sent out arrows and scattered them; He multiplied lightning flashes and threw them into turmoil.

relationship: parallel disappearance compared with a vanished dream
rationale: Isaiah likens the hostile nations' wealth to a sleeper's dream; Zophar describes an apparently established ungodly person vanishing like a dream or nighttime apparition. The comparison concerns transience, not acceptance of every claim in Zophar's speech.
source_text: Like someone dreaming in sleep will be the wealth of all nations who marched against Ariel, all who marched against Jerusalem, and all assembled against her and afflicting her.

target_units.text: For when he thinks he has become firmly established, then he will perish utterly; those who saw him will say, ‘Where is he?’
Like a dream that has flown away, he will certainly not be found; he flew off like a nighttime apparition.
An eye glanced past him and will not do so again, and his place will no longer perceive him.

relationship: close image of wicked prosperity dissolving upon awakening
rationale: Isaiah's thirsty dreamer wakes still thirsty, illustrating the hostile nations' futile wealth. The psalm describes the lawless becoming desolate and their image counted as nothing like an awakening person's dream.
source_text: They will be like people drinking and eating in sleep; when they rise, their dream is futile. As a thirsty person dreams of drinking but wakes still thirsty, his soul having hoped in vain, so will be the wealth of all nations who marched against Mount Zion.

target_units.text: How they became desolate suddenly! They failed; they perished through their lawlessness.
Like the dream of someone awakening, Lord, in Thy city Thou wilt count their image as nothing.

relationship: close description of drunkenness not caused by wine
rationale: Both explicitly describe intoxication without wine. Isaiah 29 connects it with the following spirit of stupor; Isaiah 51 places it within the cup-of-anger image and promises removal of that cup.
source_text: Grow faint, lose your senses and suffer a hangover, neither from sikera nor from wine,

target_units.text: Therefore listen, humbled one, drunk but not from wine.
Thus says the Lord God who judges His people: ‘Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of falling, the bowl of anger. You will not drink it again.

relationship: scriptural echo of a divinely given spirit of stupor
rationale: Romans speaks of God giving a spirit of stupor and eyes not to see while discussing Israel's hardened remainder. Isaiah likewise says the Lord made them drink a spirit of stupor and will close eyes, specifically including prophetic and ruling figures.
source_text: because the Lord has made you drink a spirit of stupor, and He will close their eyes and those of their prophets and rulers, those who see hidden things.

target_units.text: What, then? What Israel seeks, it did not obtain; but the chosen obtained it, and the rest were hardened,
just as it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes not to see and ears not to hear, until this very day.”

relationship: related sealing of a book that restricts access to its words
rationale: Isaiah's literate recipient cannot read because the book is sealed; Daniel is commanded to seal a book until the time of completion. Both connect a sealed book with restricted access, but only Daniel specifies that temporal limit.
source_text: All these sayings will be for you like the words of this sealed book. If they give it to a person who knows how to read, saying, “Read these,” he will say, “I cannot read, for it is sealed.”

target_units.text: But you, Daniel, cover the commands and seal the book until the time of completion, until the many go mad and the earth is filled with injustice.”

relationship: same-chapter contrast between two impediments to reading
rationale: The literate recipient in the preceding verse cannot read a sealed book; this recipient cannot read because he does not know how. The paired scenes distinguish the book's closure from the reader's inability.
source_text: This book will be given into the hands of a person who does not know how to read. Someone will say to him, “Read this,” and he will say, “I do not know how to read.”

target_units.text: All these sayings will be for you like the words of this sealed book. If they give it to a person who knows how to read, saying, “Read these,” he will say, “I cannot read, for it is sealed.”

relationship: explicit quotation of lip honor and human commandments
rationale: Jesus names Isaiah and quotes the contrast between honoring God with lips and a distant heart, followed by vain worship through human teachings. Matthew applies the words in the dispute over traditions and God's commandment.
source_text: The Lord said, “This people draws near Me; with their lips they honor Me, but their heart is far from Me. They revere Me in vain, teaching human commands and teachings.

target_units.text: Hypocrites! Isaiah prophesied well about you, saying,
‘This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me.
In vain they worship Me, teaching human commandments as teachings.’”

relationship: explicit quotation concerning the destruction of worldly wisdom
rationale: Paul quotes God's destruction of the wise people's wisdom and setting aside of discerning understanding. Isaiah connects this with removing the people; Paul places the quotation within his argument about the word of the cross.
source_text: Therefore, behold, I will proceed to remove this people; I will remove them, destroy the wise people’s wisdom and hide the discerning people’s understanding.”

target_units.text: For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will set aside the understanding of the discerning.”

relationship: parallel exposure of people who think God cannot see their deeds
rationale: Isaiah's secret counselors ask who sees or knows them; the psalm reports wrongdoers saying the Lord will not see or understand and answers by invoking the maker of eyes and ears. Both challenge supposed concealment from God.
source_text: Woe to those making deep counsel, but not through the Lord! Woe to those making counsel in secret! Their deeds will be in darkness, and they will say, “Who has seen us, and who will know us or what we do?”

target_units.text: They said, The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.
Understand now, you senseless among the people; and you fools, become wise at last.
Does the One who planted the ear not hear, or the One who formed the eye not perceive?

relationship: close potter-and-formed-object challenge applied to God
rationale: Both ask whether what is formed can answer back to its maker, using clay and a potter. Isaiah's objections concern being formed and made intelligently; Romans asks why the object was made this way and develops the potter's authority over vessels.
source_text: Will you not be reckoned as the potter’s clay? Will the formed thing say to its former, “You did not form me,” or the work to its maker, “You did not make me intelligently”?

target_units.text: But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is formed say to the One who formed it, “Why didst Thou make me this way?”
Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

relationship: close transformation language concerning Carmel and forest
rationale: Both include Carmel being reckoned as forest. Isaiah 29 first describes Lebanon changing like Carmel; Isaiah 32 first says Carmel becomes wilderness. The comparison preserves those distinct supplied transformations.
source_text: Is it not yet a little while until Lebanon is changed like Mount Chermel, and Mount Chermel is reckoned as forest?

target_units.text: until a spirit from on high comes upon you. Chermel will become wilderness, and Chermel will be reckoned as forest.

relationship: related restoration of blind sight and deaf hearing
rationale: Isaiah promises that deaf people will hear a book's words and blind eyes will see; Jesus reports blind people receiving sight and deaf people hearing among His works. Matthew does not include Isaiah's particular reference to the book.
source_text: On that day the deaf will hear a book’s words, and the blind people’s eyes in darkness and mist will see.

target_units.text: Jesus answered them, “Go and report to John what you hear and see:
the blind receive sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, the dead are raised and the poor have good news proclaimed to them.

relationship: related promise of joy for poor and distressed people
rationale: Isaiah promises the poor joy in the Lord and gladness for the hopeless; Jesus blesses the poor and promises that present weeping will become laughter. The shared reversal concerns poverty and distress, with different descriptions of the recipients.
source_text: The poor will exult with joy because of the Lord, and the hopeless among people will be filled with gladness.

target_units.text: Lifting His eyes toward His disciples, He said, “Blessed are you who are poor, because yours is God’s kingdom.
Blessed are you who hunger now, because you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, because you will laugh.

relationship: parallel disappearance of arrogant ungodly power
rationale: Isaiah declares the failure of the lawless and the disappearance of the arrogant; the psalm describes an ungodly person raised like Lebanon's cedars who can no longer be found, followed by the destruction of the lawless together.
source_text: The lawless one has failed, the arrogant one has perished, and those acting lawlessly for evil have been destroyed,

target_units.text: I saw an ungodly person raised high and lifting himself like the cedars of Lebanon.
I passed by, and behold, he was gone; I sought him, but his place could not be found.
Guard innocence and look upon uprightness, for a peaceful person has a remnant.
But the lawless will be destroyed together; the remnants of the ungodly will be destroyed.

relationship: close condemnation of hostility to gate-reproof and corrupt justice
rationale: Both join mistreatment of someone reproving at the gates with turning aside vulnerable or righteous people in judgment. Amos additionally names payments; Isaiah names people causing sin by a word.
source_text: and those who cause people to sin by a word. They will make all who reprove at the gates a stumbling block, and have turned the righteous aside through injustices.

target_units.text: They hated one who reproved at the gates and abhorred a holy word.

Therefore, because you struck the poor with fists and accepted choice gifts from them, you built houses of polished stone but certainly will not inhabit them; you planted desirable vineyards but certainly will not drink their wine.
For I knew your many impieties, and your sins are strong: trampling the righteous, taking payments and turning aside the poor at the gates.

relationship: close promise that restored Israel will not be ashamed
rationale: Isaiah 29 promises that Jacob will not now be ashamed or Israel change his face; Isaiah 45 promises Israel salvation without shame or abasement. The latter expressly gives the assurance an everlasting scope.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord concerning Jacob’s house, which He set apart from Abraham: “Jacob will not now be ashamed, nor will Israel now change his face;

target_units.text: Israel is saved by the Lord with everlasting salvation. They will not be ashamed or ever be abashed for eternity.

relationship: parallel honoring of God by Jacob's and Israel's descendants
rationale: Isaiah's children sanctify Jacob's Holy One and fear Israel's God after seeing His works; the psalm summons all Jacob's seed to glorify the Lord and all Israel's seed to fear Him. The same ancestral names frame reverent praise.
source_text: but when their children see My works, because of Me they will sanctify My name, sanctify Jacob’s Holy One and fear Israel’s God.

target_units.text: You who fear the Lord, praise Him! All Jacob’s seed, glorify Him! Let all Israel’s seed fear Him,

relationship: close restoration of understanding and stammering speech
rationale: Both connect renewed understanding or attentive minds with stammering tongues learning to speak peace. Isaiah 29 also describes grumblers learning obedience; Isaiah 32 describes the heart of the weak paying attention.
source_text: Those wandering in spirit will know understanding; grumblers will learn obedience, and stammering tongues will learn to speak peace.”

target_units.text: The heart of the weak will pay attention and listen, and stammering tongues will quickly learn to speak peace.

relationship: parallel political action undertaken without God
rationale: Isaiah condemns plans and agreements made without God or His Spirit; Hosea says they reigned for themselves rather than through God and did not make their rule known to Him. The political acts differ, but their exclusion of God is explicit.
source_text: “Woe, rebellious children,” thus says the Lord, “you made a plan not through Me and agreements not through My spirit, to add sins upon sins,

target_units.text: They reigned for themselves and not through Me; they ruled and did not make it known to Me. They made their silver and gold into idols for themselves, so that they might be destroyed.

relationship: related warning against returning to Egypt for military reliance
rationale: Isaiah condemns going to Egypt for Pharaoh's help without asking God; Deuteronomy forbids a ruler to return the people to Egypt in order to multiply horses. The legal rule and prophetic rebuke address related Egyptian dependence without identical wording.
source_text: you who go down to Egypt, but they did not ask Me, to be helped by Pharaoh and sheltered by Egyptians.

target_units.text: For he shall not multiply horses unto himself, neither shall he cause the people to return unto Egypt, that he may multiply horses unto himself; for the Lord has said: You shall not return by this way again.

relationship: parallel failure of Egypt as Israel's support
rationale: Isaiah says reliance on Pharaoh and Egypt will bring shame; Ezekiel depicts Egypt as a reed staff that shatters when Israel leans on it and injures those relying on it. Both expose Egyptian support as harmful rather than secure.
source_text: For Pharaoh’s shelter will become your shame, and reproach for those trusting in Egypt.

target_units.text: All who inhabit Egypt will know that I am the Lord, because you became a reed staff for the house of Israel.
When they took hold of you with their hand, you were crushed; and when every hand prevailed against them, and when they rested upon you, you were shattered and broke all their loins.

relationship: close criticism of Tanis's leadership
rationale: Isaiah 30 names leaders in Tanis and evil messengers laboring vainly; Isaiah 19 calls Tanis's rulers fools and describes failed counsel that leads Egypt astray. The common place and failure of its leaders support the comparison.
source_text: For there are leaders in Tanis, evil messengers; they will labor in vain

target_units.text: Tanis’s rulers will be fools; the king’s wise counselors—their counsel will become foolish. How will you say to the king, “We are sons of the discerning, sons of kings from the beginning”?
Where are your wise men now? Let them announce to you and say what the Lord Sabaoth has counseled against Egypt.
Tanis’s rulers failed, and Memphis’s rulers were exalted; they will lead Egypt astray tribe by tribe.

relationship: close warning of shame from reliance on Egypt
rationale: Isaiah warns that the approached people will provide shame instead of assistance; the surrounding verses identify Egypt. Jeremiah explicitly predicts shame from Egypt and says the Lord has rejected that hope.
source_text: toward a people that will not benefit them, neither for assistance nor for profit, but for shame and reproach.”

target_units.text: Why did you show such contempt by repeating your ways? You will also be put to shame by Egypt, as you were put to shame by Assyria.
For from here too you will go out with your hands on your head, because the Lord rejected your hope, and you will not prosper in it.

relationship: related perilous wilderness journey among serpents
rationale: Isaiah places the wealth-bearing journey amid wilderness hardship, asps and flying-asps' offspring; Deuteronomy recalls Israel led through a fearful wilderness with biting serpents, scorpions and thirst. The journeys and named creatures differ; neither passage supplies all the other's details.
source_text: The vision of the four-footed creatures in the wilderness. In affliction and hardship, a lion and lion cub from there, asps and offspring of flying asps; they carried their wealth on donkeys and camels to a nation that will not benefit them with help, but with shame and reproach.

target_units.text: who led you through that great and fearful wilderness, wherein were biting serpents, and scorpions, and thirst, where there was no water; who brought forth for you a spring of water out of the sheer rock;

relationship: parallel contrast between futile human assistance and divine help
rationale: Isaiah calls Egypt's proposed benefit empty and its consolation futile; the psalm calls human salvation vain while seeking God's help. Isaiah names a particular foreign helper, whereas the psalm states the contrast more generally.
source_text: Egyptians will benefit you with futile and empty things. Announce to them, “This consolation of yours is futile.”

target_units.text: Give us help from affliction, for human salvation is vain.
But through God we will do a mighty deed, and He will reduce our afflicters to nothing.

relationship: close instruction to preserve a message on a tablet for its appointed time
rationale: Both command a written record on a tablet and associate the message with a future appointed season. Isaiah additionally names a book and enduring preservation; Habakkuk specifies a clear inscription on boxwood and the vision's movement toward its end.
source_text: Now then, sit and write these things on a tablet and in a book, because these things will endure for days of appointed times and for ever.

target_units.text: The Lord answered me: “Write a vision clearly on a boxwood tablet, so that the one reading these things may pursue them.
For the vision is still for a season, and it will rise toward the end and not toward emptiness. If he delays, wait for him, for coming he will come and certainly will not linger.

relationship: close refusal to hear God's law and prophetic words
rationale: Isaiah calls the people disobedient and unwilling to hear God's law; Zechariah describes people refusing to listen and making their hearts disobedient toward the law and Spirit-sent prophetic words. The following Isaiah verse likewise introduces rejected prophets.
source_text: For this is a disobedient people, lying sons who did not want to hear God’s law,

target_units.text: But they refused to pay attention, turned a senseless back and made their ears heavy so as not to listen,
and made their heart disobedient, so as not to listen to My law and the words the Lord Almighty sent by His Spirit through the former prophets. Great anger came from the Lord Almighty.

relationship: close command forbidding prophets to prophesy
rationale: Isaiah's people tell prophets not to announce their message; Amos explicitly reports the command that prophets must not prophesy. Isaiah goes further by requesting another deception instead.
source_text: who say to the prophets, “Do not announce to us,” and to those seeing visions, “Do not speak to us. Instead, speak to us and announce another deception,

target_units.text: I took some of your sons as prophets and some of your young men for consecration. Are these things not so, sons of Israel?” says the Lord.
“But you gave the consecrated ones wine to drink and commanded the prophets, saying, ‘You must not prophesy!’

relationship: related pressure to replace an unwelcome prophetic message
rationale: Isaiah's audience asks for a different deceptive announcement; the messenger to Micaiah asks him to agree with favorable royal predictions. Micaiah's insistence on speaking the Lord's word supplies a contrasting response to pressure.
source_text: who say to the prophets, “Do not announce to us,” and to those seeing visions, “Do not speak to us. Instead, speak to us and announce another deception,

target_units.text: The messenger who went to call Micaiah spoke to him, saying, “Behold, all the prophets speak favorable things about the king with one mouth. Please let your words be like the words of one of them, and speak favorably.”
Micaiah said, “As the Lord lives, whatever the Lord says to me, that I will speak.”

relationship: close rejection of God together with His way
rationale: Isaiah's speakers ask that the path and Israel's Holy One be removed; Job describes someone telling the Lord to depart and refusing knowledge of His ways. Both associate rejection of God with refusal of His way, without treating Job's reported speech as an instruction.
source_text: and turn us from this way, remove this path from us, and remove Israel’s Holy One from us.”

target_units.text: Yet he says to the Lord, ‘Go away from me! I do not wish to know Thy ways.
What is the Mighty One, that we should serve Him? And what benefit is there in meeting Him?’

relationship: close reliance on falsehood as supposed protection
rationale: Isaiah 30 condemns disobedience, hope in falsehood and trust in what it calls this word; Isaiah 28 reports people making falsehood their hope and deceit their shelter. Both warnings expose the claimed basis of security before announcing its collapse.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord, Israel’s Holy One: “Because you disobeyed these words and hoped in falsehood, and because you grumbled and came to trust in this word,

target_units.text: Because you said, “We made a covenant with Hades and agreements with death; if a rushing storm passes, it will certainly not come upon us. We made falsehood our hope and will be sheltered by deceit,”

relationship: close use of a collapsing wall for deceptive security
rationale: Isaiah compares the people's sin to the imminent collapse of a wall; Ezekiel pictures false assurances of peace as a coated wall that God tears down. Both make the wall's fall disclose the failure of what people trusted.
source_text: therefore this sin will be for you like a wall falling immediately in a captured fortified city, whose fall is immediately at hand,

target_units.text: Because they misled My people, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace, and this one builds a wall, and they coat it—if it is going to fall,

say to those coating it, ‘It will fall.’ There will be a flooding downpour, and I will put stones for hurling into their bonds, and they will fall; there will be an upending wind, and it will be split.
And behold, the wall has fallen! Will they not say to you, ‘Where is your coating with which you coated it?’
Therefore thus says the Lord: I will unleash an upending blast with wrath; a flooding downpour will come in My anger, and I will bring the projectile stones in wrath for complete destruction,

and I will tear down the wall you coated, and it will fall. I will lay it upon the ground; its foundations will be uncovered, and it will fall, and you will be brought to an end with rebukes. You will recognize that I am the Lord.

relationship: close judgment image of an irreparably shattered earthen vessel
rationale: Isaiah describes a jar shattered so completely that no useful shard remains; Jeremiah smashes a jar to depict the people and city broken like a vessel that cannot be healed. Their accounts share the vessel and irreparable judgment while differing in the shard detail.
source_text: and its fall will be like the shattering of an earthen vessel, fine pieces from a jar, so that no shard is found among them with which to lift fire or draw a little water.”

target_units.text: And smash the jar before the eyes of the men going out with you,
and say: Thus says the Lord: This is how I will smash this people and this city, as an earthenware vessel is smashed that cannot be healed again.

relationship: related summons to return while relinquishing futile supports
rationale: Isaiah connects turning back with salvation and rebukes strength made futile by false trust; Hosea summons Israel to return and reject Assyria, horses and handmade gods. Hosea adds God's promise of healing and openly declared love.
source_text: Thus says the Lord, Israel’s Holy One: “When you turn back and groan, then you will be saved and know where you were. When you trusted in futile things, your strength became futile.” But you did not want to listen,

target_units.text: Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, because you grew weak in your injustices.
Take words with you and return to the Lord your God. Speak to Him so that you do not receive injustice but receive good things, and we will repay the fruit of our lips.
Assur will certainly not save us; we will not mount a horse, and we will certainly no longer call the works of our hands “Our gods.” The One in you will have mercy on an orphan.
I will heal their dwellings; I will love them openly, because My anger turned away from them.

relationship: close failure of swift flight and horses to save
rationale: Isaiah answers confidence in horses and swift mounts with flight and swift pursuers; Amos says the runner's flight and the horseman's attempt to save his life will fail. Both deny that speed and mounted strength secure escape.
source_text: but you said, “We will flee on horses.” Therefore you will flee. You said, “We will ride swift mounts.” Therefore those pursuing you will be swift.

target_units.text: and flight will perish from the runner, the mighty one will certainly not maintain his strength, and the fighter will certainly not save his life,
and the archer will certainly not stand, the swift of foot will certainly not be saved, nor will the horseman save his life,

relationship: close numerical picture of many fleeing before very few
rationale: Isaiah says a thousand flee at one voice and many at five; Deuteronomy asks how one pursues a thousand and two put tens of thousands to flight unless God has delivered them up. The numerical disproportion corresponds without harmonizing the second number.
source_text: At the voice of one, a thousand will flee; at the voice of five, many will flee, until you are left like a mast upon a mountain, like someone carrying a standard upon a hill.

target_units.text: How shall one pursue a thousand, and two put tens of thousands to flight, unless God had sold them, and the Lord had delivered them up?

relationship: related divine delay directed toward mercy
rationale: Isaiah says God waits to show pity and is exalted to have mercy; Second Peter explains the Lord's apparent delay as patience aimed at repentance rather than people's perishing. The latter concerns the promised coming rather than Isaiah's immediate restoration setting.
source_text: Again God will wait to pity you, and therefore He will be exalted to have mercy on you, because the Lord our God is a judge. Where will you leave your glory? Blessed are those remaining in Him.

target_units.text: The Lord is not slow concerning the promise, as some consider slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing anyone to perish but all to come to repentance.

relationship: close hearing of distressed prayer in Zion's restoration
rationale: Isaiah describes Jerusalem's bitter plea and God's hearing and mercy; the psalm joins rebuilding Zion with attention to lowly prayer and hearing the groaning of captives, so His name is proclaimed in Zion and Jerusalem.
source_text: For a holy people will dwell in Zion, and Jerusalem wept bitterly, “Have mercy on me!” He will have mercy on you at the sound of your cry; when He saw, He listened to you.

target_units.text: for the Lord will build Zion and will appear in His glory.
He looked upon the prayer of the lowly and did not treat their petition as nothing.
Let this be written for another generation, and the people being created will praise the Lord,
for He leaned out from His holy height; the Lord looked from heaven upon the earth,
to hear the groaning of those in bonds, to release the sons of those put to death,
to announce the Lord’s name in Zion and His praise in Jerusalem,

relationship: close language of bread of affliction
rationale: Isaiah names bread of affliction and scant water; the order concerning Micaiah names bread and water of affliction. The expressions connect severe deprivation, while the agents and the source's additional warning about misleaders differ.
source_text: The Lord will give you bread of affliction and scant water; those misleading you will certainly no longer approach you, for your eyes will see those misleading you,

target_units.text: say to put this man in prison and have him eat bread of affliction and water of affliction until I return in peace.”

relationship: parallel speech from people who lead others astray
rationale: The surrounding Isaiah wording identifies the speakers behind the hearers as those who led them astray, even as they announce a way to walk. Jeremiah condemns false dreamers whose spoken lies lead the people astray. This preserves Isaiah's misleaders rather than converting them into faithful teachers.
source_text: and your ears will hear the words of those behind you who led you astray, saying, “This is the way; let us walk in it, whether right or left.”

target_units.text: Behold, I am against the prophets who prophesy false dreams, who told them and led My people astray by their lies and wanderings. I did not send or command them, and they will bring this people no benefit at all.

relationship: close destruction and dispersal of a manufactured idol
rationale: Isaiah describes removing silver- and gold-covered idols, reducing them to fine pieces and winnowing them away; Moses grinds the calf fine and scatters it upon water. Exodus additionally describes burning and drinking, which are not imported into Isaiah.
source_text: You will remove the silver-covered and gold-covered idols, reduce them to fine pieces and winnow them like a menstruating woman’s fluid; like dung you will push them away.

target_units.text: He took the calf they had made, burned it in the fire, ground it fine, scattered it on the water, and made the sons of Israel drink it.

relationship: close promise of rain, produce and abundant bread
rationale: Both join rain for the land with plentiful produce and satisfying bread. Isaiah additionally describes a fertile spacious pasture for livestock; Leviticus links its agricultural abundance with obedience to God's ordinances.
source_text: Then there will be rain for your land’s seed; bread from your land’s produce will be plentiful and rich, and on that day your livestock will graze a fertile, spacious place,

target_units.text: then I will give you rain in its season. The land shall yield its produce, and the trees of the fields shall yield their fruit.
And your threshing shall reach the grape harvest, and the grape harvest shall reach the sowing. You shall eat your bread to satisfaction and dwell securely in your land.

relationship: related provision of food for working cattle
rationale: Isaiah's cattle that work the earth receive prepared straw and barley; Deuteronomy forbids muzzling an ox while it treads grain. The former describes provision and the latter regulates labor, but both concern feeding cattle engaged in agricultural work.
source_text: your bulls and cattle working the earth will eat straw prepared with barley and winnowed.

target_units.text: You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.

relationship: related promised water flowing across the restored land
rationale: Isaiah promises flowing water on high mountains and hills; Joel describes flowing water at Judah's outlets and a spring from the Lord's house. Both place the new flow on the announced day, with different terrain and sources of water.
source_text: On every high mountain and every lofty hill there will be flowing water on that day, when many perish and towers fall.

target_units.text: On that day mountains will drip sweetness, hills will flow with milk, and all Judah’s water outlets will flow with water. A spring will come out of the Lord’s house and water the Wadi of Rushes.

relationship: related transformation of light in the people's restoration
rationale: Isaiah 30 intensifies the moon's and sun's light on the day God heals His people; Isaiah 60 makes the Lord the everlasting light and promises an end to mourning. The latter does not repeat the sevenfold solar measure or treat the two descriptions as identical.
source_text: The moon’s light will be like the sun’s light, and the sun’s light will be sevenfold on the day when the Lord heals His people’s fracture; He will heal the pain of your wound.

target_units.text: The sun will not be your light by day, nor will the rising moon light your night. Instead, the Lord will be your everlasting light and God your glory.
For your sun will not set, and your moon will not fail. The Lord will be your everlasting light, and your days of mourning will be fulfilled.

relationship: related divine utterance accompanied by consuming fire
rationale: Isaiah joins the Lord's angry utterance with wrath consuming like fire; Jeremiah receives God's words as fire in his mouth, with the people as wood to be devoured. Both associate divine speech with consuming fire; Jeremiah explicitly makes the words themselves fire.
source_text: Behold, the Lord’s name comes after a long time, wrath burning. His lips’ utterance comes with glory, an utterance full of anger, and the anger of His wrath will consume like fire.

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Almighty: Because you spoke this utterance, behold, I have made My words fire in your mouth, and this people wood, and it will devour them.

relationship: related divine judgment portrayed as an overwhelming flood
rationale: Isaiah 30 likens God's spirit to water sweeping through a ravine to the neck; Isaiah 8 describes the Lord bringing a mighty river identified with Assyria's king, whose encampment fills the country. Isaiah 8 does not contain the neck detail in this supplied wording.
source_text: His spirit will come like water sweeping through a ravine, reaching the neck, and will divide to trouble nations in futile wandering. Delusion will pursue them and seize them in their faces.

target_units.text: therefore, behold, the Lord brings up against you the river’s strong and abundant water—the king of the Assyrians and his glory. He will ascend every ravine of yours and walk over every wall of yours,
and he will remove from Judea a person able to lift a head or someone strong enough to accomplish anything. His encampment will fill the breadth of your country. God is with us.”

relationship: related festive approach to God's holy place
rationale: Isaiah asks about continual festival-like entry with rejoicing and a flute to the Lord's mountain; the psalm speaks of passing to God's house with exultation, thanksgiving and a celebrating sound. The question is not converted into the psalmist's declaration of intention.
source_text: Must you always rejoice and always enter My holy places like festival-keepers, like people rejoicing as they enter with a flute to the Lord’s mountain, to Israel’s God?

target_units.text: These things I remembered and poured out my soul within me: for I will pass through the place of a wonderful tent to God’s house, with a voice of exultation and thanksgiving, a celebrating sound.

relationship: close divine voice accompanied by hail, fire and lightning
rationale: Isaiah joins God's glorious voice with consuming flame, lightning, water and hail; the psalm likewise joins hail and fire with the Lord's thunderous voice and multiplied lightning. These are related descriptions of His forceful intervention.
source_text: God will make His voice’s glory heard and show His arm’s wrath with fury, anger and consuming flame. He will strike violently with lightning, like water and hail falling together violently.

target_units.text: From the far-shining radiance before Him, the clouds passed— hail and coals of fire.
And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave His voice.
And He sent out arrows and scattered them; He multiplied lightning flashes and threw them into turmoil.

relationship: historical counterpart to the Lord's defeat of Assyria
rationale: Isaiah announces the Assyrians' defeat by the Lord's voice and blow; Kings narrates the Lord's angel striking their camp and Sennacherib withdrawing. The narrative supplies the angelic action rather than explicitly repeating the voice image.
source_text: For at the Lord’s voice the Assyrians will be defeated by the blow with which He strikes them.

target_units.text: By night the Lord’s angel went out and struck one hundred eighty-five thousand in the Assyrians’ camp. When they rose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead bodies.
Sennacherib king of the Assyrians departed, went away, returned, and lived in Nineveh.

relationship: related battle scene joined with music
rationale: Isaiah describes opponents turning to fight with flutes and a lyre; Chronicles places appointed singers and thanksgiving before the enemy forces turn upon one another. The campaigns and musical descriptions differ, so this is a related conjunction of battle and music rather than an identification.
source_text: It will be all around him, from where he hoped for help, on which he himself relied; they will turn and fight him with flutes and a lyre.

target_units.text: He consulted the people and appointed psalm singers and those giving praise, to give thanks and praise the holy things as they went out before the army. They said, “Give thanks to the Lord, for His mercy is for ever.”
When His praise of thanksgiving began, the Lord set the sons of Ammon to fight against Moab and Mount Seir, who had come out against Judah, and they were routed.
The sons of Ammon and Moab rose against Mount Seir’s inhabitants to destroy and wipe them out. When they had finished Seir’s inhabitants, they rose against one another to be destroyed.

relationship: parallel divine judgment described with fire and sulfur
rationale: Isaiah compares the Lord's wrath with a ravine burning with sulfur; Genesis narrates sulfur and fire from the Lord overthrowing Sodom and Gomorrah. The ravine and cities remain distinct, and Isaiah's unnamed location is not replaced with either city.
source_text: For you will be called to account ahead of time. Has it also been prepared for you to rule a deep ravine, with wood laid out, fire and much wood? The Lord’s wrath is like a ravine burning with sulfur.

target_units.text: And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of the heaven;
and He overthrew those cities, and all the surrounding country, and all that lived in the cities, and all that sprang from the earth.

relationship: close contrast between chariot-and-horse confidence and reliance on God
rationale: Isaiah rebukes trust in Egypt's many horses and chariots instead of Israel's Holy One; the psalm contrasts reliance on chariots and horses with being magnified in the Lord's name. Both explicitly oppose military equipment to divine reliance.
source_text: Woe to those going down to Egypt for help, trusting in horses and chariots because there are many, and in horses, a very great multitude, but not trusting Israel’s Holy One or seeking God!

target_units.text: These rely on chariots, and those on horses, but we will be magnified in the name of the Lord our God.
They were fettered and fell, but we rose and were set upright.

relationship: related royal prohibition behind Egyptian horse reliance
rationale: Deuteronomy forbids multiplying horses by returning the people to Egypt; Isaiah condemns going down to Egypt for help and trusting its numerous horses. The law supplies a specific Egypt-and-horses prohibition, while Isaiah adds the failure to seek God.
source_text: Woe to those going down to Egypt for help, trusting in horses and chariots because there are many, and in horses, a very great multitude, but not trusting Israel’s Holy One or seeking God!

target_units.text: For he shall not multiply horses unto himself, neither shall he cause the people to return unto Egypt, that he may multiply horses unto himself; for the Lord has said: You shall not return by this way again.

relationship: close assurance that divine counsel and word stand
rationale: Isaiah 31 says God's word will not be set aside as He acts against evil; Isaiah 46 declares that all His counsel will stand and that He has spoken and acted. The different announced actions share the certainty of His effective word.
source_text: He Himself, wise, brought evils upon them; His word will certainly not be set aside. He will rise against evil people’s houses and against their futile hope,

target_units.text: announcing the last things beforehand, before they came to be—and together they were fulfilled. I said, ‘All My counsel will stand, and I will do everything I have planned,’
calling a bird from the east and from a distant land concerning what I have planned. I spoke and brought it about; I created and acted. I brought him and made his journey prosper.

relationship: close rejection of fleshly human support in place of God
rationale: Isaiah contrasts Egypt's human being and horses' flesh with God and denies their help; Jeremiah curses hope placed in a human and the flesh of his arm when the heart leaves the Lord. Jeremiah also states the contrasting blessing of trust in God.
source_text: an Egyptian human being and not God, horses’ flesh, with no help. The Lord will bring His hand against them; the helpers will grow weary, and all will perish together.

target_units.text: Cursed is the person who places his hope in a human and will rest the flesh of his arm upon him, and whose heart departs from the Lord;
and he will be like a wild tamarisk in the wilderness; he will not see when good things come, and will dwell among salt-plants and in a wilderness, in a salt land that is not inhabited.
And blessed is the person who has trusted in the Lord, and the Lord will be his hope;

relationship: related portrayal of the Lord as a fierce lion
rationale: Isaiah compares the Lord's descent upon Zion's mountains with a lion crying over prey; Hosea portrays the Lord as a lion to Judah's house that seizes beyond rescue. The passages share the fierce predator image without equating the purposes of the two interventions.
source_text: For thus the Lord said to me: “As a lion or lion cub cries over prey it has caught and shouts over it until the mountains fill with its voice, and they are defeated and terrified by the greatness of its wrath, so the Lord Sabaoth will descend to march upon Mount Zion, upon her mountains.

target_units.text: For I am like a panther to Ephraim and like a lion to Judah’s house. I seize and will go away and take, and there will be no one to rescue.

relationship: close avian image of protection for Jerusalem
rationale: Isaiah compares the Lord shielding and saving Jerusalem with flying birds; Jesus describes His wish to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers chicks under her wings. Matthew also records the city's unwillingness, which is absent from Isaiah's assurance here.
source_text: Like flying birds, so the Lord will shield Jerusalem, rescue, preserve and save.”

target_units.text: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her! How often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!

relationship: close summons for lawless planners to return
rationale: Isaiah 31 addresses those planning a deep lawless plan and commands them to turn back; Isaiah 55 tells the lawless man to forsake his counsels and return to the Lord for mercy. Both connect repentance with abandoning wrongful plans.
source_text: Turn back, you planning a deep and lawless plan.

target_units.text: let the ungodly forsake his ways, and the lawless man his counsels; and let him return to the Lord, and he will receive mercy; for He will abundantly forgive your sins.

relationship: close abandonment of handmade silver and gold idols
rationale: Both announce a day when people reject the silver and gold objects they made. Isaiah 2 names casting them toward worthless ones and bats; Isaiah 31 emphasizes renouncing the works of their hands.
source_text: For on that day people will renounce their silver and golden handmade things, which their hands made.

target_units.text: For on that day a person will cast out his silver and gold abominations, which they made to worship, to the worthless ones and the bats,

relationship: legal counterpart to rejection of silver and gold gods
rationale: Exodus explicitly forbids making gods of silver or gold; Isaiah announces renunciation of the silver and golden handmade objects. The command identifies the prohibited manufacture, while the prophecy describes abandoning its products.
source_text: For on that day people will renounce their silver and golden handmade things, which their hands made.

target_units.text: You shall not make gods of silver for yourselves, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves.

relationship: historical counterpart to Assyria defeated beyond human weaponry
rationale: Isaiah announces Assour falling without a human sword and fleeing; Kings narrates the Lord's angel striking the Assyrian camp and Sennacherib withdrawing. The target concerns the camp's supernatural defeat, not the later separate account of the king's death by his sons.
source_text: Assour will fall. Neither a man’s sword nor a human’s sword will devour him, and he will flee, but not from a sword. The young men will be defeated,

target_units.text: By night the Lord’s angel went out and struck one hundred eighty-five thousand in the Assyrians’ camp. When they rose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead bodies.
Sennacherib king of the Assyrians departed, went away, returned, and lived in Nineveh.

relationship: related blessing of family life in Zion and Jerusalem
rationale: Isaiah blesses the person with seed in Zion and household members in Jerusalem; the psalm joins blessing from Zion, Jerusalem's good things and seeing children's children. The familial and geographical elements correspond without repeating the preceding military imagery.
source_text: for they will be enclosed by a rock as by a palisade and defeated, and the fugitive will be captured. Thus says the Lord: “Blessed is the one who has seed in Zion and household members in Jerusalem.”

target_units.text: May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see Jerusalem’s good things all the days of your life.
And may you see sons of your sons. Peace upon Israel.

relationship: close promise of a righteous king exercising judgment
rationale: Isaiah announces a righteous king and rulers judging rightly; Jeremiah announces a righteous rising for David, a king doing judgment and righteousness. Jeremiah expressly supplies the Davidic connection and the name Josedek, which this Isaiah verse does not name.
source_text: For behold, a righteous king will reign, and rulers will rule with judgment.

target_units.text: Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up a righteous rising for David. A king will reign and understand, doing judgment and righteousness upon the earth.
In his days Judah will be saved and Israel will dwell confidently. This is his name, which the Lord will call him: Josedek.

relationship: related image of abundant water in a thirsty land
rationale: The man's appearance in Zion is compared with a rushing river glorious in a thirsty land; Isaiah 41 promises rivers, springs and watercourses where land is thirsty. The comparison concerns the water image, not the source's separate statements about concealed words and hiding.
source_text: The man will conceal his words and hide as from rushing water; he will appear in Zion like a rushing river, glorious in a thirsty land.

target_units.text: but will open rivers on mountains and springs amid plains. I will make the wilderness marshes and the thirsty land watercourses,

relationship: close refusal to place trust in human beings
rationale: Isaiah says the people will cease trusting human beings and listen; the psalm commands against trusting rulers and human beings without salvation and blesses hope in God. The psalm adds human mortality as its reason.
source_text: They will no longer trust in human beings, but will give their ears to listen.

target_units.text: Do not trust in rulers and in sons of men who have no salvation.
His spirit will go out, and he will return to his earth; on that day all their reasonings will perish.
Happy the one whose Helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God,

relationship: close renewed understanding and stammering tongues speaking peace
rationale: Both associate changed understanding with stammering tongues learning to speak peace. Isaiah 32 speaks of weak hearts paying attention; Isaiah 29 additionally describes wandering spirits and grumblers learning obedience.
source_text: The heart of the weak will pay attention and listen, and stammering tongues will quickly learn to speak peace.

target_units.text: Those wandering in spirit will know understanding; grumblers will learn obedience, and stammering tongues will learn to speak peace.”

relationship: contrast concerning a fool's elevation to authority
rationale: Isaiah promises that people will no longer tell the fool to rule; Ecclesiastes observes the evil of a fool being placed at great heights. The prophecy reverses a kind of misordering described by the wisdom observation.
source_text: They will no longer tell the fool to rule, and your attendants will no longer say, “Be silent.”

target_units.text: the fool was set in great heights, while the rich will sit in a low place.

relationship: close connection of foolish heart, corrupt speech and wrongdoing
rationale: Isaiah describes the fool's heart thinking futile things and speaking deception toward the Lord amid lawless acts; the psalm joins the fool's heart denying God with corrupt practices and deceitful tongues. Isaiah additionally specifies harm to hungry and thirsty souls.
source_text: For the fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will think futile things, carrying out lawless acts and speaking deception toward the Lord, scattering hungry souls and making thirsty souls empty.

target_units.text: For the end. A psalm of David. A fool said in his heart, “There is no God.” They acted corruptly and became abominable in their practices; there is no one who shows kindness; there is not even one.
The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God.

All turned aside; together they became useless; there is no one who shows kindness, not even one. Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they practiced deceit. The venom of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood; brokenness and misery are in their ways, and they did not know a way of peace. There is no fear of God before their eyes.

relationship: legal contrast to unjust words that destroy the lowly
rationale: Isaiah condemns counsel that destroys lowly people through unjust words in judgment; Exodus forbids perverting a poor person's case, unrighteous charges and gifts that corrupt righteous words. The law directly opposes the judicial abuse described.
source_text: For evil people’s counsel will devise lawless things, to destroy the lowly with unjust words and scatter the lowly people’s words in judgment.

target_units.text: You shall not pervert the judgment of a poor man in his cause.
You shall keep far away from every unrighteous charge; the innocent and the righteous you shall not kill, neither shall you justify the ungodly for gifts.
And you shall receive no gifts; for gifts blind the eyes of those who see, and corrupt righteous words.

relationship: related permanence of wise or divine counsel
rationale: Isaiah says the devout person's wise counsel will remain; Proverbs contrasts many human reasonings with the Lord's counsel remaining forever. The holders of the counsel differ; the comparison does not identify every human plan with God's counsel.
source_text: The devout made wise plans, and this counsel will remain.

target_units.text: Many are the reasonings in a man’s heart, but the counsel of the Lord remains for ever.

relationship: related warning to affluent daughters before humiliation
rationale: Isaiah 32 addresses wealthy women and daughters living in hope before announcing grief and sackcloth; Isaiah 3 addresses Zion's exalted daughters and describes the removal of luxurious adornment. The shared setting is confident women confronted with the loss of comfort.
source_text: Wealthy women, rise and hear my voice! Daughters in hope, hear my words!

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: “Because Zion’s daughters were exalted and walked with high neck and glancing eyes, dragging their tunics as their feet moved and playing with their feet,
God will humble Zion’s ruling daughters, and the Lord will uncover their appearance
on that day, and the Lord will remove the glory of their clothing and their ornaments, hair braids, fringes and crescents,
the necklace and the adornment of their face,
the arrangement of glorious adornment, armlets, bracelets, a hair braid, armbands, rings and earrings,
the garments bordered with purple and those purple at the center,
the coverings used about the house and the transparent Laconian garments,
the fine-linen, blue-purple and scarlet garments, and fine linen interwoven with gold and blue-purple, and trailing summer wraps.

Instead of sweet fragrance there will be dust; instead of a belt you will gird yourself with a cord; instead of golden head adornment you will have baldness because of your deeds; instead of the tunic with purple at its center you will gird yourself with sackcloth.

relationship: close lament over exhausted vintage and failed cultivation
rationale: Isaiah announces the end of the vintage and sowing; Joel describes damaged grain, dried wine, a perished harvest and a dried vine. Both describe ruined agricultural provision; Joel also says human beings put joy to shame.
source_text: Remember the days of a year in pain with hope; the vintage has been exhausted, the sowing has ceased and will certainly no longer come.

target_units.text: because the plains have suffered. Let the earth mourn, because grain has suffered, wine has dried up, and oil has diminished.
The farmers have dried up. Lament, estates, over wheat and barley, because the harvest from the field has perished.
The vine has dried up and the fig trees have diminished; pomegranate, palm, apple tree and all the field’s trees have dried up, because human beings have put joy to shame.

relationship: close call to mourning through sackcloth
rationale: Isaiah calls confident women to grieve, undress and wrap sackcloth around their waists; Joel commands priestly ministers to lament and sleep in sackcloth because offerings have ceased. The recipients differ, but the prescribed mourning garment and agricultural context correspond.
source_text: Be dismayed, grieve, you confident women; undress, become naked and wrap sackcloth around your waists,
