target_units.text: Wrap yourselves and beat your breasts, priests; lament, ministers of the altar! Enter and sleep in sackcloth, ministers of God, because sacrifice and drink offering have been kept away from your God’s house.

relationship: close breast-beating and lament over damaged fields and vines
rationale: Isaiah commands breast-beating over the desirable field and fruitful vine; Joel laments the failed field harvest and dried vine and commands priests to beat their breasts. The same mourning action is tied to agricultural loss, without equating the two addressed groups.
source_text: and beat your breasts because of the desirable field and fruitful vine.

target_units.text: The farmers have dried up. Lament, estates, over wheat and barley, because the harvest from the field has perished.
The vine has dried up and the fig trees have diminished; pomegranate, palm, apple tree and all the field’s trees have dried up, because human beings have put joy to shame.

Wrap yourselves and beat your breasts, priests; lament, ministers of the altar! Enter and sleep in sackcloth, ministers of God, because sacrifice and drink offering have been kept away from your God’s house.

relationship: close growth of thorns upon the people's devastated land
rationale: Isaiah 32 says the people's earth will grow thorns and grass as joy leaves houses; the vineyard oracle announces abandonment and thorns and identifies the vineyard with Israel's house. The latter supplies a vineyard parable rather than the city's houses.
source_text: My people’s earth will grow thorn and grass, and joy will be removed from every house. Wealthy city,

target_units.text: Now I will announce to you what I will do to My vineyard: I will remove its fence, and it will be plundered; I will pull down its wall, and it will be trampled,
and I will abandon My vineyard. It will certainly not be pruned or dug, and thorns will rise in it as in fallow ground. I will command the clouds not to rain upon it.
For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is Israel’s house, and the man of Judah a beloved new planting. I waited for it to produce judgment, but it produced lawlessness, not righteousness but an outcry.

relationship: parallel abandoned settlements becoming animal habitat
rationale: Isaiah depicts abandoned houses and villages becoming caves and wild donkeys' delight; Jeremiah announces Jerusalem as a dwelling of dragons and Judah's cities without inhabitants. The animals and locations retain their distinct descriptions.
source_text: houses abandoned! They will leave the city’s wealth and desirable houses; villages will become caves for ever, wild donkeys’ delight, pastures for shepherds,

target_units.text: And I will give Jerusalem over to deportation and as a dwelling of dragons, and make Judah’s cities disappear, so that they are not inhabited.

relationship: related promise of a spirit coming upon the hearers
rationale: Isaiah says a spirit from on high will come upon the people; Jesus promises power when the Holy Spirit comes upon His disciples for witness. Acts does not repeat Isaiah's supplied transformation of Carmel into wilderness and forest.
source_text: until a spirit from on high comes upon you. Chermel will become wilderness, and Chermel will be reckoned as forest.

target_units.text: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem and [in] all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.”

relationship: close righteousness and judgment filling a restored place
rationale: Isaiah 32 places judgment in the wilderness and righteousness in Carmel; Isaiah 33 describes Zion filled with judgment and righteousness. The same paired qualities characterize different named places within the restoration language.
source_text: Judgment will rest in the wilderness, and righteousness will dwell in Carmel.

target_units.text: Holy is God, who dwells on high; Zion has been filled with judgment and righteousness.

relationship: close connection between righteousness and peace
rationale: Isaiah makes peace the work of righteousness and associates righteousness with enduring rest; James describes a fruit of righteousness sown in peace for peacemakers. The texts connect the same qualities while describing their relation in different directions.
source_text: The works of righteousness will be peace; righteousness will secure rest, and they will be confident for ever.

target_units.text: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, considerate, open to persuasion, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, without hypocrisy.
And a fruit of righteousness is sown in peace for those who make peace.

relationship: close promise of peaceful dwelling without fear
rationale: Isaiah promises a city of peace, confident living and restful wealth; Ezekiel promises peaceful dwelling on the land, sleep in the woods and freedom from terror. The settings differ, but secure habitation is the shared promised result.
source_text: His people will dwell in a city of peace and live confidently, and they will rest with wealth.

target_units.text: I will make a covenant of peace with David and remove harmful beasts from the land. They will dwell in the wilderness and sleep in the woods.
I will place them around My mountain and give you rain, rain of blessing.

The trees in the plain will give their fruit, and the land will give its strength. They will dwell upon their land in hope of peace and know that I am the Lord when I shatter their yoke. I will rescue them from the hand of those who enslaved them.
They will no longer be plunder for the nations, and the land’s beasts certainly will no longer eat them. They will dwell in hope, and no one will terrify them.

relationship: historical counterpart to protection from destructive hail
rationale: Isaiah promises that descending hail will not come upon the addressed people; Exodus distinguishes hail-struck Egypt from Goshen, where the sons of Israel experienced no hail. The comparison concerns a protected population, not identity of the two storms.
source_text: If hail comes down, it will not come upon you. Those dwelling in the forests will be confident like those in the plain.

target_units.text: Throughout Egypt the hail struck people and livestock. It struck every plant in the plains and shattered all the trees there.
Only in the land of Goshen, where the sons of Israel were, was there no hail.

relationship: related blessing expressed through growth beside water
rationale: Isaiah blesses those sowing beside every water; the psalm calls the person devoted to God's law blessed and likens him to a tree planted beside water outlets. The shared watered-growth image differs from Isaiah's sowers, ox and donkey.
source_text: Blessed are those sowing beside every water, where ox and donkey tread!

target_units.text: Blessed is the man who did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, and did not stand in the way of sinners, and did not sit in the seat of pestilent men;
but his will is in the Lord’s law, and on His law he will meditate day and night.
He will be like the tree planted beside the outlets of waters, which will give its fruit in its season, and whose leaf will not fall off; and everything he does will be prospered.

relationship: close moth-and-garment image for the defeat of opponents
rationale: Isaiah 33 ends by comparing the rejecters' defeat with a moth upon a cloak; Isaiah 50 addresses those who might harm the speaker as growing old like a garment and being devoured like a moth. The recurring garment-and-moth comparison is specific, without resolving the unusual afflicting and rejecting clauses earlier in Isaiah 33:1.
source_text: Woe to those afflicting you—yet no one afflicts you—and the one rejecting you does not reject. The rejecters will be captured and handed over; like a moth upon a cloak, so they will be defeated.

target_units.text: Behold, the Lord helps me. Who will harm me? Behold, all of you will grow old like a garment, and it will devour you like a moth.

relationship: close salvation in affliction for those who trust the Lord
rationale: Isaiah seeks mercy because the speakers trust God and names salvation in affliction; the psalm calls the Lord the righteous people's defender in affliction and says He saves them because they hope in Him. Isaiah separately contrasts a disobedient seed's destruction.
source_text: Lord, have mercy on us, for we have trusted in Thee. The disobedient people’s seed came to destruction, but our salvation is in a time of affliction.

target_units.text: But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, and He is their defender in a time of affliction.
The Lord will help them and rescue them; He will remove them from sinners and save them, because they have hoped in Him.

relationship: related divine sound joined with the scattering of opponents
rationale: Isaiah describes peoples dismayed and nations scattered at God's terrifying sound; the psalm joins the Lord's thunderous voice with arrows that scatter and lightning that throws opponents into turmoil. The psalm names weapons and lightning that this verse leaves unstated.
source_text: At the sound of Thy terror, peoples were dismayed by fear of Thee, and nations scattered.

target_units.text: And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave His voice.
And He sent out arrows and scattered them; He multiplied lightning flashes and threw them into turmoil.

relationship: close exaltation of the holy God with judgment and righteousness in Zion
rationale: Both connect the Lord's holiness and exaltation with Zion and the paired qualities judgment and righteousness. The psalm speaks of what He has done in Jacob; Isaiah describes Zion filled with those qualities.
source_text: Holy is God, who dwells on high; Zion has been filled with judgment and righteousness.

target_units.text: The Lord is great in Zion and exalted above all the peoples.
Let them give thanks to Thy great name, for it is fearsome and holy.
The King’s honor loves judgment. Thou didst prepare uprightness; judgment and righteousness in Jacob Thou hast done.
Exalt the Lord our God and bow down at His footstool, for He is holy.

relationship: close association of treasure with wisdom, knowledge and fear of the Lord
rationale: Isaiah names wisdom, knowledge and reverence toward the Lord among treasures of righteousness; Proverbs tells the hearer to seek wisdom like treasure and promises knowledge of God and understanding of His fear. The treasury image and three associated gifts connect the texts.
source_text: They will be handed over under law; our salvation is among treasures. There are wisdom, knowledge and reverence toward the Lord; these are treasures of righteousness.

target_units.text: and if you seek it like silver and search it out like treasures,
then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God.
For the Lord gives wisdom, and from His presence come knowledge and understanding.

relationship: related delegation seeking peace under threat of war
rationale: Isaiah describes fearful messengers pleading and weeping for peace; Jesus' comparison describes a king sending a delegation for peace when facing a stronger force. Luke's scene is illustrative and does not include Isaiah's tears.
source_text: Behold, in your terror they themselves will fear; those you feared will fear you. For messengers will be sent asking for peace, weeping bitterly, pleading for peace.

target_units.text: Or what king, going to meet another king in war, will not first sit down and consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet the one coming against him with twenty thousand?
And if not, while the other is still far away, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.

relationship: close personification of the earth mourning
rationale: Both explicitly say that the earth mourned in an account of devastation. Isaiah 33 adds Lebanon's shame, Sharon becoming marshes and Galilee and Carmel becoming visible; those details are not replaced by Isaiah 24's description of the inhabited world's destruction.
source_text: The earth mourned; Lebanon was ashamed; Sharon became marshes. Galilee and Carmel will be clearly visible.

target_units.text: The earth mourned, the inhabited world was destroyed, and the earth’s high ones mourned.

relationship: close divine declaration that now He will arise
rationale: Both place the words now I will arise in the Lord's mouth. Isaiah adds His glorification and exaltation; the psalm specifies the misery and groaning of poor and needy people as the occasion for intervention.
source_text: “Now I will rise,” says the Lord. “Now I will be glorified; now I will be exalted.

target_units.text: “Because of the misery of the poor and because of the groaning of the needy, now I will arise,” says the Lord. “I will set him in salvation; I will speak openly in him.”

relationship: parallel consuming fire against opponents under divine wrath
rationale: Isaiah warns that the strength of the hearers' spirit will be futile and fire will consume them; the psalm describes enemies made like a fiery furnace as the Lord's anger throws them into turmoil and fire devours them. The target does not repeat Isaiah's statement about their spirit.
source_text: Now you will see, now you will perceive; your spirit’s strength will be futile. Fire will consume you.

target_units.text: You will make them like a fiery furnace at the time of your presence; the Lord in His anger will throw them into turmoil, and fire will devour them.

relationship: close image of opponents burned like discarded thorns
rationale: Isaiah compares the burning of nations with a thorn thrown in a field and burned; David's concluding words describe the lawless through cast-out thorn imagery and their burning in shame. The shared combustible-thorn comparison preserves the different addressed groups.
source_text: Nations will be burned, like a thorn thrown in a field and burned.

target_units.text: For is not my house so with the Mighty One? He established an everlasting covenant with me, ready at every time, guarded; for all my salvation and every desire—surely the lawless one will not sprout.
All of them are like a thorn cast out, for they will not be taken in the hand,
and a man will not toil among them—and full of iron and a spear’s shaft; they will be utterly burned with fire in their shame.”

relationship: related recognition of God's deeds and power
rationale: Isaiah predicts that distant hearers will hear His deeds and those near will know His strength; the psalm invites people to see God's works and describes His power and regard for nations. The psalm supplies sea-and-river examples rather than Isaiah's near-and-far distinction.
source_text: Those far away will hear what I did; those drawing near will know My strength.”

target_units.text: Come and see God’s works, fearsome in His counsels concerning the sons of men,
He who turns the sea into dry land; through a river they will pass on foot. There we will rejoice in Him,
who rules the age by His power; His eyes look upon the nations. Let those provoking Him not exalt themselves within themselves. Diapsalma.

relationship: related fear before divine fire
rationale: Isaiah describes trembling among the ungodly and asks who will announce the burning fire and everlasting place; Hebrews urges reverence and awe because God is a consuming fire. The comparison does not recast Isaiah's question as one about dwelling in everlasting burnings.
source_text: The lawless in Zion departed; trembling will seize the ungodly. Who will announce to you that fire burns? Who will announce to you the everlasting place?

target_units.text: Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be grateful, and through this gratitude serve God acceptably with reverence and awe,
for indeed our God is a consuming fire.

relationship: close ethical description of the person permitted secure dwelling
rationale: Both describe righteous walking, truthful or straight speech and refusal of gifts associated with injustice. The psalm asks who can dwell with God, while Isaiah's following verse promises the described person secure rocky shelter.
source_text: One walking in righteousness, speaking a straight way, hating lawlessness and injustice, shaking his hands free of gifts, making his ears heavy so as not to hear a judgment of blood, and closing his eyes so as not to see injustice,

target_units.text: A psalm of David. Lord, who will sojourn in Thy dwelling, and who will encamp on Thy holy mountain?
One who walks blamelessly and works righteousness, speaking truth in his heart,
who did not act deceitfully with his tongue, nor do evil to his neighbor, and did not take up reproach against those nearest him.
One who acts wickedly is held in contempt before him, but he honors those who fear the Lord; one who swears to his neighbor and does not set it aside.
He did not lend his silver at interest and did not take gifts against innocent people. The one who does these things will never be shaken.

relationship: legal counterpart to refusing gifts and bloodshed in judgment
rationale: Isaiah's righteous person shakes off gifts and refuses a judgment of blood; Exodus forbids unjust charges, killing the innocent and receiving gifts that corrupt justice. The law supplies concrete prohibitions corresponding to the ethical portrait.
source_text: One walking in righteousness, speaking a straight way, hating lawlessness and injustice, shaking his hands free of gifts, making his ears heavy so as not to hear a judgment of blood, and closing his eyes so as not to see injustice,

target_units.text: You shall not pervert the judgment of a poor man in his cause.
You shall keep far away from every unrighteous charge; the innocent and the righteous you shall not kill, neither shall you justify the ungodly for gifts.
And you shall receive no gifts; for gifts blind the eyes of those who see, and corrupt righteous words.

relationship: close divine provision of elevated rocky shelter
rationale: Isaiah promises a high cave of strong rock for the righteous person; the psalm describes the Lord hiding the speaker in trouble and raising him upon a rock. The psalm uses a tent as well, whereas Isaiah adds assured bread and water.
source_text: this one will dwell in a high cave of strong rock. Bread will be given him, and his water is trustworthy.

target_units.text: For He hid me in a tent in the day of my troubles; He sheltered me in the hiding place of His tent; He raised me upon a rock.

relationship: historical example of protected life supplied with bread and water
rationale: Isaiah promises bread and trustworthy water in secure shelter; the Lord sends Elijah into hiding, provides water from a wadi and commands ravens that bring bread. The narrative supplies a particular example of divine sustenance rather than identifying Elijah with Isaiah's unnamed person.
source_text: this one will dwell in a high cave of strong rock. Bread will be given him, and his water is trustworthy.

target_units.text: “Go from here eastward and hide yourself at the Chorrath wadi, which faces the Jordan.
You will drink water from the wadi, and I will command the ravens to sustain you there.”
Elijah acted according to the Lord’s word and stayed at the Chorrath wadi facing the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread in the morning and meat in the evening, and he drank water from the wadi.

relationship: related sight of a glorious king
rationale: Isaiah 33 promises sight of a king with glory; Isaiah 6 describes the Lord enthroned amid glory and explicitly says the prophet's eyes saw the King, the Lord Sabaoth. The later promise does not repeat that full identification in its own sentence.
source_text: You will see a king with glory, and your eyes will see a land from afar.

target_units.text: In the year that King Oziah died, I saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and lifted up; and the house was full of His glory.
And seraphim stood around Him: each one had six wings, and each one had six wings; with two they covered their faces, and with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew.
And one cried to another, saying: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord Sabaoth; all the earth is full of His glory.
And the lintel was lifted at the sound of their cry, and the house was filled with smoke.
And I said, Woe is me, for I am pierced to the heart! For I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips; and my eyes have seen the King, the Lord Sabaoth.

relationship: close rhetorical questioning of learned authorities
rationale: Isaiah asks where scholars, counselors and the one counting those fed are; Paul asks where the wise person, scribe and debater are when exposing worldly wisdom. The repeated where-questions address learned authority while retaining the different lists.
source_text: Your soul will ponder fear: “Where are the scholars? Where are the counselors? Where is the one counting those being fed,

target_units.text: Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made the world’s wisdom foolish?

relationship: close restoration imagery of a secure city's tent, ropes and pegs
rationale: Isaiah 33 describes Jerusalem as unshaken tents with immovable pegs and unbroken ropes; Isaiah 54 commands widening the tent, lengthening ropes and strengthening pegs for expansion. Stability and enlargement are distinct uses of the shared civic tent image.
source_text: Behold, Zion, the city, our salvation! Your eyes will see Jerusalem, a wealthy city, tents that will certainly not be shaken; her tent’s pegs will never be moved, nor her ropes torn.

target_units.text: “Widen the place of your tent and your curtains. Pitch them; do not spare! Lengthen your ropes and strengthen your pegs.
Spread out still farther to right and left. Your offspring will inherit nations, and you will settle deserted cities.

relationship: related abundant water in a holy setting with restricted passage
rationale: Isaiah describes broad rivers and canals where people and rowing ships will not pass; Ezekiel's water from the house becomes a torrent that cannot be crossed. Isaiah's excluded traffic is not given Ezekiel's explicit explanation of violently surging water.
source_text: For the Lord’s name is great for you. There will be a place for you, rivers and broad, spacious canals. You will not go this way, nor will a rowing ship go.

target_units.text: He brought me to the house’s vestibules, and look—water was flowing out beneath the open court toward the east, for the house’s front faced east. The water was descending from the right side, from the south toward the altar.
He brought me out by the north gate and led me around outside to the court’s gate facing east. Look—the water was flowing down from the right side.
As the man went out opposite, with a measure in his hand, he measured a thousand with the measure and went through the water—water of release.
He measured a thousand and went through water up to the thighs. He measured a thousand and went through water up to the waist.
He measured a thousand and could not go through, for the water surged violently like the rush of a torrent that they will not cross.

relationship: close divine authority to judge and save
rationale: Isaiah calls the Lord judge, ruler, king and Savior; James identifies the one Lawgiver and Judge able to save and destroy. Both attribute judgment and saving power to God, with different additional titles and actions.
source_text: For my God is great; the Lord will not pass me by. The Lord is our judge, the Lord our ruler, the Lord our king; this One will save us.

target_units.text: There is one Lawgiver and Judge, the One able to save and destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?

relationship: related maritime collapse exposing strength to loss
rationale: Isaiah describes torn ropes, a tilted mast and a vessel handed over for plunder; Ezekiel portrays a great maritime city shattered at sea, its forces and trading company falling with it. The nautical failures correspond without identifying Isaiah's vessel with Tyre.
source_text: Your ropes tore because it was not strong; your mast tilted. It will not lower the sails or raise a signal until it is handed over for plunder. Then many lame people will take spoil.

target_units.text: Your rowers led you in much water; the south wind shattered you in the heart of the sea.

There were your forces, your payment and that of your mixed companies, your rowers and pilots, your counselors and your mixed companies from your mixed companies, all your warrior men in you, and your whole assembly within you; they will fall in the heart of the sea on the day of your fall.

relationship: related participation in spoil despite limited ability to fight
rationale: Isaiah promises spoil even to many lame people; David insists that men too weak to continue the pursuit share the spoils equally with fighters. The bodily limitations differ, but both passages include people who could otherwise be excluded from victory's gains.
source_text: Your ropes tore because it was not strong; your mast tilted. It will not lower the sails or raise a signal until it is handed over for plunder. Then many lame people will take spoil.

target_units.text: David came to the two hundred men who had grown too weak to follow David and whom he had seated at the Bosor torrent. They came out to meet David and the people with him. David approached the people, and they asked him about his welfare.

Every pestilent and evil man among the warriors who had gone with David answered. They said, “Because they did not pursue with us, we will give them none of the spoils we rescued. Let each take only his wife and children and return.”
David said, “You must not do this, after the Lord has given to us and guarded us. The Lord delivered into our hands the geddour that came against us.

Who would listen to these words of yours? For they are no less than you. As is the share of the one who goes down into war, so shall be the share of the one who stays with the equipment. They shall share equally.”
From that day onward, it became a command and a rule for Israel, until today.

relationship: related forgiveness joined with relief from bodily frailty
rationale: Isaiah links the inhabitants' not saying they are weary with forgiven sin; the psalm joins God's gracious treatment of lawless deeds with healing and renewed youth. The comparison preserves Isaiah's weariness rather than replacing it with the psalm's diseases.
source_text: The people dwelling among them will certainly not say, “I am weary,” for their sin has been forgiven.

target_units.text: who is gracious toward all your lawless deeds, who heals all your diseases;
who redeems your life from corruption, who crowns you with mercy and compassions;
who fills your desire with good things; your youth will be renewed like an eagle’s.

relationship: close universal summons to nations and the world's inhabitants
rationale: Both call all nations and the world's inhabitants to hear. Isaiah explicitly includes rulers and the earth; the psalm extends the address through rich and poor and different descriptions of human beings.
source_text: Draw near, nations, and hear, rulers! Let the earth and those in it hear, the inhabited world and the people in it!

target_units.text: Hear these things, all nations; give ear, all who inhabit the world,
both the earthborn and the sons of men, rich and poor together.

relationship: close universal outpouring of divine wrath upon nations
rationale: Isaiah announces the Lord's wrath and slaughter against all nations; Zephaniah describes His judgment upon assembled nations and kings, pouring out furious wrath as the earth is consumed. The forms of destruction differ, but the international scope and divine anger are explicit.
source_text: For the Lord’s wrath is against all nations, and anger against their number, to destroy them and hand them over to slaughter.

target_units.text: Therefore wait for Me, says the Lord, for the day of My rising for testimony. My judgment is for assemblies of nations, to receive kings and pour all My furious wrath upon them; for all the earth will be consumed in My jealous fire.

relationship: related rising decay and stench after an enemy's defeat
rationale: Isaiah describes exposed dead whose odor rises; Joel describes the expelled northern force's decay and stench rising. Isaiah adds mountains soaked with blood, while Joel supplies the force's movement toward the seas and waterless land.
source_text: Their wounded and dead will be thrown out; their odor will rise, and mountains will be soaked with their blood.

target_units.text: and I will drive away from you the one from the north and thrust it into a waterless land. I will make its front disappear into the first sea and its rear into the last sea; its decay will rise, and its stench will rise, because it magnified its deeds.”

relationship: close judgment imagery of stars falling from heaven
rationale: Isaiah describes heaven rolled like a scroll and stars falling like leaves; Jesus' discourse likewise describes stars falling and heavenly powers shaken. Mark does not reproduce the scroll, vine or fig-leaf comparisons.
source_text: Heaven will roll up like a scroll, and all the stars will fall like leaves from a vine, like leaves falling from a fig tree.

target_units.text: But in those days, after that distress, the sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light.
The stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.

relationship: related divine sword carrying out judgment
rationale: Isaiah depicts the Lord's sword descending against Idumea; Deuteronomy describes His sharpened sword and repayment against enemies. Deuteronomy makes the arrows drunk with blood, whereas Isaiah says the sword became drunk in heaven.
source_text: My sword became drunk in heaven. Behold, it will descend upon Idumea and upon the people of destruction, with judgment.

target_units.text: For I will sharpen My sword as lightning, and My hand shall lay hold of judgment; and I will repay a penalty unto the enemies, and unto them that hate Me will I repay.
I will make My arrows drunk with blood, and My sword shall devour flesh, from the blood of the slain and of captives, from the head of the rulers of the enemies.

relationship: close portrayal of divine judgment as the Lord's sacrifice
rationale: Isaiah names the Lord's sacrifice and slaughter in Bosor and Idumea; Zephaniah announces His prepared sacrifice and judgment upon rulers and the king's house. Their sacrificial judgment images concern different named settings and add different details.
source_text: The Lord’s sword was filled with blood, thickened with lambs’ fat and the fat of male goats and rams, for the Lord has a sacrifice in Bosor and a great slaughter in Idumea.

target_units.text: Revere the Lord God, for the Lord’s day is near. The Lord has prepared His sacrifice and consecrated His invited guests.
On the day of the Lord’s sacrifice I will exact judgment upon the rulers, the king’s house and all wearing foreign clothes.

relationship: close sacrificial slaughter imagery joining cattle, fat and blood
rationale: Isaiah's rams and bulls fall as the earth becomes drunk with blood and full of fat; Ezekiel's great sacrifice joins rulers and warriors with fattened cattle and drinking blood to drunkenness. Isaiah makes the earth drunk and full; Ezekiel gives the eating and drinking to summoned birds and beasts.
source_text: The stout ones will fall with them, and rams and bulls; the earth will become drunk with blood and be filled with their fat.

target_units.text: And you, son of man, say, Thus says the Lord: Say to every flying bird and all the plain’s beasts, Gather and come! Gather from all those around to My sacrifice that I have sacrificed for you, a great sacrifice upon Israel’s mountains. You will eat flesh and drink blood.
You will eat giants’ flesh and drink the blood of the land’s rulers: rams, calves and male goats, and the calves all fattened.
You will eat fat to fullness and drink blood to drunkenness from My sacrifice that I sacrificed for you.
At My table you will be filled with horse and rider, giant and every warrior, says the Lord.

relationship: close pairing of a day of recompense and a year of divine action
rationale: Isaiah 34 announces a day of judgment and year of repayment for Zion; Isaiah 63, also naming Edom and Bosor, announces a day of recompense and year of redemption. The repeated time-pair and Edomite setting connect the oracles without equating repayment with redemption.
source_text: For it is the Lord’s day of judgment and a year of repayment for Zion’s judgment.

target_units.text: Who is this arriving from Edom, with redness of garments from Bosor, so beautiful in His robe, with force and strength? “I speak righteousness and saving judgment.”
Why are Thy garments red and Thy clothes as though from a trodden winepress?
“I am full of what has been trodden. No man from the nations is with Me. I trampled them in wrath, crushed them like earth, and brought their blood down to earth.
For a day of recompense came upon them, and a year of redemption is here.

relationship: related destruction of land through sulfur and fire
rationale: Isaiah transforms ravines and earth into burning pitch and sulfur; Genesis narrates sulfur and fire overthrowing Sodom, Gomorrah and their surrounding country. Genesis does not include pitch or identify its cities with Idumea.
source_text: Her ravines will turn to pitch, her earth to sulfur, and her land will burn like pitch

target_units.text: And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of the heaven;
and He overthrew those cities, and all the surrounding country, and all that lived in the cities, and all that sprang from the earth.

relationship: close judgment fire that will not be quenched
rationale: Isaiah 34 describes enduring unquenched fire and smoke over deserted land; Isaiah 66 depicts the unquenched fire associated with the limbs of people who transgressed against God. The comparison concerns unquenchable judgment, not identical locations or victims.
source_text: night and day. It will not be quenched for an everlasting time, and her smoke will rise upward. For generations and a long time she will be deserted.

target_units.text: ‘They will go out and see the limbs of the people who transgressed against Me, for their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched. They will be a spectacle to all flesh.’

relationship: close desolated places occupied by wild creatures
rationale: Isaiah's desolated territory houses hedgehogs, ravens and other creatures; Zephaniah depicts Nineveh as a wasteland with hedgehogs, ravens and wild animals in its structures. The respective creature lists and places remain distinct.
source_text: Birds, hedgehogs, ibises and ravens will dwell in her; a measuring cord for deserted land will be cast upon her, and donkey-centaurs will dwell in her.

target_units.text: He will stretch His hand against the north and destroy the Assyrian, making Nineveh a waterless wasteland like a wilderness.

Flocks and all the wild animals of the earth will graze within her; chameleons and hedgehogs will lie in her recessed panels. Wild animals will cry in her openings, and ravens in her gateways, for cedar is her structure.

This is the contemptuous city dwelling in confidence, saying in her heart, “I am, and there is no one after me.” How she became a wasteland, pasture for wild animals! Everyone passing through her will hiss and wave his hands.

relationship: related destruction of Idumea's leading and powerful people
rationale: Isaiah announces the disappearance of the land's rulers, kings and magnates; Obadiah announces the loss of Idumea's wise people and terror among Teman's warriors. The same Edomite setting supports the comparison while the classes of leaders differ.
source_text: Her rulers will be no more, for her kings, her rulers and her magnates will come to destruction.

target_units.text: On that day, says the Lord, I will destroy the wise from Idumea and understanding from Mount Esau.
Your warriors from Teman will be terrified, so that a person may be removed from Mount Esau,

relationship: close thorns growing in abandoned dwellings
rationale: Isaiah describes thorny trees rising in cities and fortifications; Hosea predicts thorns in the people's dwellings after their departure. Isaiah additionally names sirens and ostriches, which Hosea does not supply.
source_text: Thorny trees will sprout in their cities and her fortifications; she will become a dwelling for sirens and a courtyard for ostriches.

target_units.text: Therefore look, they will go away from Egypt’s misery; Memphis will receive them, and Machmas will bury them. Destruction will inherit their silver; thorns will be in their dwellings.

relationship: close uncanny inhabitants of ruined places
rationale: Both passages place demons and donkey-centaurs in desolated territory. Isaiah 34 describes meeting, calling and resting; Isaiah 13 describes demons dancing and donkey-centaurs dwelling in Babylon. The creatures recur without collapsing the different cities or actions.
source_text: Demons will meet donkey-centaurs and cry one to another. There donkey-centaurs will rest, for they found rest for themselves.

target_units.text: Wild beasts will rest there, and the houses fill with sound; sirens will rest there, and demons dance there.
Donkey-centaurs will dwell there, and hedgehogs make nests in their houses. It comes quickly and will not delay.

relationship: close image of hedgehogs nesting amid desolation
rationale: Isaiah 34 describes a hedgehog nesting and its children kept safe by the earth; Isaiah 13 names hedgehogs making nests in abandoned houses. Only Isaiah 34 adds the meeting deer and the protection of the young.
source_text: There a hedgehog nested, and the earth kept her children safe. There deer met and saw one another’s faces;

target_units.text: Donkey-centaurs will dwell there, and hedgehogs make nests in their houses. It comes quickly and will not delay.

relationship: related gathering of animals under divine command
rationale: Isaiah attributes the animals' complete gathering to the Lord's command and His spirit; Genesis describes animals entering Noah's ark in pairs as God commanded him. The places, purpose and pairing differ, and Genesis does not identify the gathering agency as the Spirit.
source_text: they passed by in number, and not one of them perished; none sought another, for the Lord commanded them and His spirit gathered them.

target_units.text: Of the birds, the clean animals, the unclean animals, and all the creeping things upon the earth,
two by two they entered the ark with Noah, male and female, as God had commanded him.

relationship: related allotment of land through a lot before God
rationale: Isaiah depicts God casting lots and apportioning grazing; Joshua's surveyors describe the land in seven portions before Joshua casts lots before the Lord. The comparison concerns the allotment method, not an identification of the different recipients.
source_text: He Himself will cast lots for them, and His hand apportioned grazing. You will inherit for an everlasting time; for generations of generations they will rest upon her.

target_units.text: The men rose and went. Joshua commanded the men going to survey the land, saying, “Go and survey the land and return to me. Here at Shiloh I will bring out a lot for you before the Lord.”
They went, surveyed the land, saw it, and wrote it by its cities in seven portions in a scroll, which they brought to Joshua.
Joshua cast a lot for them at Shiloh before the Lord.

relationship: close image of restoration as blossoming like a lily
rationale: Isaiah summons the thirsty wilderness to flower like a lily; Hosea promises that Israel will blossom like a lily under God's dew. Both use the same flower for renewed life, with different grammatical subjects and means of watering.
source_text: Rejoice, thirsty wilderness! Let the wilderness exult and flower like a lily,

target_units.text: I will be like dew to Israel; he will blossom like a lily and put down his roots like Lebanon.

relationship: close transfer of Lebanon's glory to a restored place
rationale: Isaiah 35 gives Lebanon's glory to the flowering wilderness; Isaiah 60 says Lebanon's glory will come in named trees to glorify God's holy place. The repeated glory phrase connects the restoration imagery without making the locations identical.
source_text: and the Jordan’s desert places will flower and exult. Lebanon’s glory and Carmel’s honor were given to her, and My people will see the Lord’s glory and God’s height.

target_units.text: Lebanon’s glory will come to you in cypress, pine, and cedar together, to glorify My holy place.

relationship: close promise that the Lord's glory will become visible
rationale: Isaiah 35 promises that God's people will see the Lord's glory; Isaiah 40 declares that His glory will be seen and all flesh will see God's salvation. The latter extends the audience and explicitly names salvation as the second object seen.
source_text: and the Jordan’s desert places will flower and exult. Lebanon’s glory and Carmel’s honor were given to her, and My people will see the Lord’s glory and God’s height.

target_units.text: And the glory of the Lord will be seen, and all flesh will see the salvation of God; for the Lord has spoken.

relationship: close exhortation to strengthen weakened hands and knees
rationale: Hebrews repeats the paired drooping hands and weakened knees as an exhortation after its discussion of discipline. Isaiah addresses limp hands and paralyzed knees before announcing God's saving intervention; Hebrews adds straight tracks for the feet.
source_text: Be strong, limp hands and paralyzed knees!

target_units.text: Therefore straighten the drooping hands and the weakened knees,
and make straight tracks for your feet, so that what is lame may not be dislocated, but rather healed.

relationship: close announcement of God's coming with recompense and reassurance
rationale: Both call the hearers not to fear and announce their God coming with strength or repayment. Isaiah 35 expressly promises salvation; Isaiah 40 places the announcement in good news to Zion and the cities of Judah.
source_text: Give encouragement, you fainthearted in mind. Be strong; do not fear! Behold, our God repays judgment and will repay; He Himself will come and save us.

target_units.text: Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good news to Jerusalem. Lift up; do not fear. Say to the cities of Judah, Behold your God!
Behold, the Lord comes with might, and His arm with dominion; behold, His reward is with Him, and His work before Him.

relationship: related restoration of sight and hearing among Jesus' works
rationale: Isaiah promises opened blind eyes and hearing ears for the deaf; Jesus reports to John's messengers that blind people receive sight and deaf people hear. Matthew includes other works and does not explicitly name Isaiah in that reply.
source_text: Then blind people’s eyes will open, and deaf people’s ears will hear.

target_units.text: Jesus answered them, “Go and report to John what you hear and see:
the blind receive sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, the dead are raised and the poor have good news proclaimed to them.

relationship: narrative counterpart to the lame person leaping
rationale: Isaiah announces a lame person leaping like a deer; Acts describes the healed man leaping, standing and walking after Peter raises him in Jesus' name. Acts does not use the deer comparison or include Isaiah's water imagery.
source_text: Then the lame person will leap like a deer, and the tongue of those with difficulty speaking will be clear, for water burst out in the wilderness and a ravine in a thirsty land,

target_units.text: Taking him by the right hand, he raised him up. At once his feet and ankles were strengthened.
Leaping up, he stood and began walking. He entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.

relationship: narrative counterpart to difficult speech becoming clear
rationale: Isaiah promises that the tongue of those with difficulty speaking will become clear; Mark narrates a man with difficulty speaking whose tongue is loosened and who speaks correctly after Jesus acts. This connection concerns the speech clause rather than the separate lame-person clause.
source_text: Then the lame person will leap like a deer, and the tongue of those with difficulty speaking will be clear, for water burst out in the wilderness and a ravine in a thirsty land,

target_units.text: They brought Him a man who was deaf and had difficulty speaking, and begged Him to lay His hand on him.
Taking him aside privately, away from the crowd, He put His fingers into his ears, spat, and touched his tongue.
Looking up to heaven, He sighed and said to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened.”
Immediately his ears were opened, the bond of his tongue was loosened, and he spoke correctly.

relationship: close transformation of dry land into marshes and flowing water
rationale: Both describe wilderness or waterless land becoming marshes and thirsty land receiving abundant water. Isaiah 35 additionally gives the birds a glad dwelling of reeds and marshes, while Isaiah 41 names rivers and springs.
source_text: the waterless place will become marshes, and a water spring will be in the thirsty land. There will be birds’ gladness, a dwelling of reeds and marshes.

target_units.text: but will open rivers on mountains and springs amid plains. I will make the wilderness marshes and the thirsty land watercourses,

relationship: close exclusion of uncleanness from restored holy passage
rationale: Isaiah 35 describes a Holy Way on which no unclean person passes; Isaiah 52 tells holy Jerusalem that no uncircumcised and unclean person will pass through her again. The road and city are distinct settings of the shared exclusion.
source_text: There will be a clean road, called a Holy Way. No unclean person will ever pass there, nor will there be an unclean way there; the scattered will walk upon it and will certainly not wander.

target_units.text: Awake, awake, Zion! Clothe yourself with your strength, Zion, and put on your glory, Jerusalem, holy city. No uncircumcised and unclean person will pass through you again.

relationship: close safety through removal of harmful wild beasts
rationale: Isaiah's redeemed travelers encounter no lion or evil wild beast on the way; Ezekiel promises removal of harmful beasts, safe dwelling and freedom from being eaten by the land's animals. The protected journey and settled land remain distinct.
source_text: No lion will be there, nor will any evil wild beast ever go up on it or be found there; instead, the redeemed will walk in it.

target_units.text: I will make a covenant of peace with David and remove harmful beasts from the land. They will dwell in the wilderness and sleep in the woods.
I will place them around My mountain and give you rain, rain of blessing.

The trees in the plain will give their fruit, and the land will give its strength. They will dwell upon their land in hope of peace and know that I am the Lord when I shatter their yoke. I will rescue them from the hand of those who enslaved them.
They will no longer be plunder for the nations, and the land’s beasts certainly will no longer eat them. They will dwell in hope, and no one will terrify them.

relationship: close recurring promise of joyful return to Zion
rationale: Both describe people brought back through the Lord, coming to Zion with everlasting gladness, praise upon their heads and the flight of pain, grief and sighing. The sustained sequence establishes a close verbal counterpart rather than a general shared hope.
source_text: Those gathered through the Lord will return and come to Zion with gladness, everlasting gladness above their heads; for praise and exultation are upon their heads, and gladness will overtake them. Pain, grief and groaning have fled.

target_units.text: and ransomed? For by the Lord they will be brought back and come to Zion with joy and everlasting exultation. Exultation and praise are upon their heads; joy will overtake them. Pain, sorrow, and sighing fled.

relationship: parallel narrative of Sennacherib's capture of Judah's fortified cities
rationale: Both date the Assyrian invasion to Hezekiah's fourteenth year and report Sennacherib capturing Judah's fortified cities. The shared ruler, date and action establish the narrative counterpart.
source_text: In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians came up against Judea’s fortified cities and took them.

target_units.text: In King Hezekiah’s fourteenth year, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians went up against Judah’s fortified cities and captured them.

relationship: parallel narrative of the Assyrian delegation at the upper pool
rationale: Both send the Assyrian spokesman from Lachish to Jerusalem with a large force and place him at the upper pool's aqueduct beside the Fuller's Field road. Kings additionally names two other envoys; Isaiah names Rapsakes alone here.
source_text: The king of the Assyrians sent Rapsakes from Lachis to Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah, with a large force. He stood at the upper pool’s aqueduct, on the road of the fuller’s field.

target_units.text: The king of the Assyrians sent Tharthan, Raphis, and Rhapsakes from Lachish to King Hezekiah against Jerusalem with a great force. They went up, came to Jerusalem, and stood at the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road of the Fuller’s Field.

relationship: related reuse of the pool and Fuller's Field meeting place
rationale: The Assyrian envoy stands by the pool and Fuller's Field road where Isaiah was earlier sent to meet Achaz. The earlier encounter brings prophetic reassurance, while this scene begins an Assyrian challenge to Hezekiah; the supplied descriptions of the pool and road are retained.
source_text: The king of the Assyrians sent Rapsakes from Lachis to Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah, with a large force. He stood at the upper pool’s aqueduct, on the road of the fuller’s field.

target_units.text: The Lord said to Isaiah, “Go out to meet Achaz, you and the remaining Jasub, your son, toward the pool of the upper road of the fuller’s field,

relationship: parallel narrative of the three Judean officials meeting the envoy
rationale: Both name Eliakim son of Chelkias, Somnas the scribe and Asaph's son as the officials who come out. Isaiah's Joach and Kings' Joash retain their respective supplied name forms and recording office.
source_text: Eliakim son of Chelkias, the steward, Somnas the scribe, and Joach son of Asaph, the record-keeper, went out to him.

target_units.text: They called to Hezekiah. Eliakim son of Chelkias the steward, Somnas the scribe, and Joash son of Asaph the recorder went out to him.

relationship: parallel challenge to Hezekiah's confidence
rationale: Both introduce the spokesman's demand in the name of the great Assyrian king and ask what confidence Hezekiah relies upon. The question opens the same narrated confrontation.
source_text: Rapsakes said to them, “Tell Hezekiah: Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians: ‘What do you trust in?

target_units.text: Rhapsakes said to them, ‘Tell Hezekiah: Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians: What is this confidence in which you trust?

relationship: parallel challenge concerning lip-words, counsel and wartime trust
rationale: Both place counsel and words of lips concerning war beside the demand to identify Hezekiah's trusted support. Isaiah frames the first clause as a question about a battle line; Kings reports a claim about counsel and strength.
source_text: Does a battle line arise through counsel or words of lips? Now whom have you trusted, that you disobey me?

target_units.text: You said—only words of lips!—“Counsel and strength for war.” Now then, in whom do you trust, that you have broken with me?

relationship: parallel narrative comparison of Egypt with a broken reed staff
rationale: Both identify Egypt as a broken reed that enters the hand of anyone leaning on it and apply the comparison to reliance on Pharaoh. The source's warning is part of the Assyrian envoy's speech.
source_text: Behold, you trust this broken reed staff, Egypt. Whoever leans on it, it will enter his hand. Such are Pharaoh king of Egypt and all who trust in him.

target_units.text: Now behold, you have put your trust in this broken reed staff, Egypt. If a man supports himself on it, it enters his hand and pierces it. So is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust him.

relationship: close Egyptian reed-staff image spoken in a different setting
rationale: Ezekiel's divine oracle also calls Egypt a reed staff that shatters when Israel leans on it and causes injury. Isaiah places the image in the Assyrian spokesman's rhetoric; the shared image does not endorse everything else he claims.
source_text: Behold, you trust this broken reed staff, Egypt. Whoever leans on it, it will enter his hand. Such are Pharaoh king of Egypt and all who trust in him.

target_units.text: All who inhabit Egypt will know that I am the Lord, because you became a reed staff for the house of Israel.
When they took hold of you with their hand, you were crushed; and when every hand prevailed against them, and when they rested upon you, you were shattered and broke all their loins.

relationship: parallel introduction of reliance on the Lord as a possible answer
rationale: Both introduce the answer that the Judeans trust the Lord their God. Kings continues with an allegation about Hezekiah's removal of high places and altars, which this brief Isaiah unit does not include.
source_text: But if you say, “We trust the Lord our God,”

target_units.text: Since you said to me, “We trust the Lord God,” is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed, saying to Judah and Jerusalem, “Before this altar you shall bow down in Jerusalem”?

relationship: parallel taunt offering two thousand horses
rationale: Both offer two thousand horses from the Assyrian master on condition that the Judeans supply riders. The identical number and condition make the mockery a specific narrative parallel.
source_text: now join with my master, the king of the Assyrians, and I will give you two thousand horses, if you can provide riders for them.

target_units.text: Now join yourselves to my master, the king of the Assyrians. I will give you two thousand horses if you can provide riders for them.

relationship: parallel challenge about one governor and Egyptian military support
rationale: Both ask how Hezekiah can face even one district governor and refer to reliance on Egyptian mounted forces. Kings calls the governor one of the master's least servants; Isaiah's additional sentence calls those trusting Egypt for horses and riders servants.
source_text: How can you face even one district governor? Those trusting Egyptians for horses and riders are servants.

target_units.text: How can you turn back the face of one district governor, one of my master’s least servants? Yet you hope in Egypt for chariots and horsemen!

relationship: parallel rhetorical claim about the Lord's authorization of the invasion
rationale: Both ask whether the Assyrians came against the country without the Lord. Kings adds the spokesman's explicit assertion that the Lord told him to attack; Isaiah's supplied verse ends with the rhetorical question.
source_text: Now have we come up without the Lord against this country to wage war upon it?’”

target_units.text: Now have we come up without the Lord against this place to destroy it? The Lord said to me, “Go up against this land and destroy it.”’

relationship: parallel request to use Syrian rather than Judean
rationale: Both have the Judean officials request Syrian, which they understand, and object to speaking Judean within the hearing of the people on the wall. The language choice and concern about the listening population correspond closely.
source_text: Eliakim, Somnas and Joach said to him, “Speak Syrian to your servants, for we understand, and do not speak Judean to us. Why do you speak within hearing of the people on the wall?”

target_units.text: Eliakim son of Chelkias, Somnas, and Joash said to Rhapsakes, ‘Please speak to your servants in Syrian, for we understand it. Do not speak with us in Judean. Why are you speaking within the hearing of the people on the wall?’

relationship: parallel siege threat directed toward the people on the wall
rationale: Both reject the officials' attempt to restrict the message and threaten the wall's population with eating dung and drinking urine alongside them. The degrading food-and-drink threat is retained as the envoy's speech, not approved instruction.
source_text: Rapsakes said to them, “Has my master sent me to your master or to you to speak these words? Was it not to the people sitting on the wall, so that they eat dung and drink urine together with you?”

target_units.text: Rhapsakes said to them, ‘Has my master sent me to speak these words to your master and to you? Was it not to the men sitting on the wall, who are to eat their own dung and drink their own urine together with you?’

relationship: parallel public proclamation in Judean
rationale: Both describe the Assyrian spokesman standing and crying loudly in Judean, commanding the population to hear the great king's words. The public choice of language follows the rejected request for Syrian.
source_text: Rapsakes stood and cried in a loud voice in Judean: “Hear the words of the great king, the king of the Assyrians:

target_units.text: Rhapsakes stood and cried out loudly in Judean: ‘Hear the words of the great king of the Assyrians!

relationship: parallel warning not to rely on Hezekiah's words for rescue
rationale: Both tell the people not to accept Hezekiah's reassuring words and deny rescue. Isaiah uses deception language, while Kings warns against being lifted up with words and explicitly mentions rescue from the Assyrian king's hand.
source_text: Thus says the king: ‘Do not let Hezekiah deceive you with words, which will not be able to rescue you,

target_units.text: Thus says the king: Do not let Hezekiah lift you up with words, for he cannot rescue you from my hand.

relationship: parallel rejection of Hezekiah's promised divine deliverance
rationale: Both report and reject the claim that God will rescue the people and prevent the city being handed to Assyria. This records the invader's challenge rather than adopting his denial as the narrative's conclusion.
source_text: and do not let Hezekiah tell you, “God will rescue you, and this city will certainly not be handed into the king of the Assyrians’ hand.”

target_units.text: Do not let Hezekiah make you hope in the Lord by saying, “The Lord will surely rescue us; this city will certainly not be handed into the hand of the king of the Assyrians.”

relationship: parallel offer of vines, figs and cistern water for surrender
rationale: Both invite the population to come out to the Assyrian king and promise household produce and cistern water. Isaiah says to eat from the vine and fig trees; Kings says to drink from the vine and eat from the fig tree.
source_text: Do not listen to Hezekiah. Thus says the king of the Assyrians: If you wish to be blessed, come out to me; each will eat from his vine and fig trees, and you will drink your cistern’s water,

target_units.text: Do not listen to Hezekiah, for thus says the king of the Assyrians: Make a blessing with me and come out to me. Each man shall drink from his vine, eat from his fig tree, and drink water from his cistern,

relationship: contrast between an invader's offer and promised undisturbed dwelling
rationale: The Assyrian envoy offers each person's vine and fig trees as an inducement to come out; Micah promises people resting beneath their own vine and fig tree without fear, guaranteed by the Lord. The familiar domestic abundance image is voiced by different authorities for different purposes.
source_text: Do not listen to Hezekiah. Thus says the king of the Assyrians: If you wish to be blessed, come out to me; each will eat from his vine and fig trees, and you will drink your cistern’s water,

target_units.text: Each will rest beneath his vine and each beneath his fig tree, and there will be no one causing fear, because the mouth of the Lord Almighty has spoken these things.

relationship: parallel promise of removal to a land like Judah
rationale: Both promise relocation to a land like the people's own, naming grain, wine, bread and vineyards. Kings adds oil-bearing olives, honey and an assurance of life, which Isaiah's shorter list does not include.
source_text: until I come and take you to a land like your land, a land of grain, wine, bread and vineyards.

target_units.text: until I come and take you to a land like your own, a land of grain, wine, bread, and vineyards, a land of oil-bearing olives and honey. You will live and certainly not die. Do not listen to Hezekiah, because he deceives you, saying, “The Lord will rescue us.”

relationship: parallel challenge comparing the Lord's rescue with the nations' gods
rationale: Both warn against Hezekiah's claim that God will rescue them and ask whether the nations' gods rescued their own lands from Assyria. Kings spans the transition across two verses; the challenge remains the Assyrian speaker's argument.
source_text: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, saying, “Your God will rescue you.” Have the nations’ gods each rescued his own country from the king of the Assyrians’ hand?

target_units.text: until I come and take you to a land like your own, a land of grain, wine, bread, and vineyards, a land of oil-bearing olives and honey. You will live and certainly not die. Do not listen to Hezekiah, because he deceives you, saying, “The Lord will rescue us.”
Have the gods of the nations ever rescued, each his own country, from the hand of the king of the Assyrians?

relationship: parallel list of captured cities used to taunt their gods
rationale: Both name the gods of Aimath, Arphath or Arphad, and Seppharim or Seppharouain, then challenge their ability to rescue Samaria. The respective native name forms remain unchanged.
source_text: Where is the god of Aimath and Arphath? Where is the god of Seppharim’s city? Were they able to rescue Samaria from my hand?

target_units.text: Where is the god of Aimath and Arphad? Where is the god of Seppharouain? And have they rescued Samaria from my hand?

relationship: parallel final challenge to Jerusalem's divine rescue
rationale: Both ask which nations' gods rescued their lands and use that claim to question Jerusalem's rescue by God. This repeats the historical opponent's inference without identifying the Lord with the gods he invokes.
source_text: Which of all these nations’ gods rescued his land from my hand, that God should rescue Jerusalem from my hand?’”

target_units.text: Who among all the gods of the lands has rescued their lands from my hand, that the Lord should rescue Jerusalem from my hand?’

relationship: parallel obedience to the king's command of silence
rationale: Both narrate that the Judeans do not answer the spokesman because their king ordered silence. The explicit command explains the identical public response.
source_text: They were silent, and no one answered him a word, because the king had ordered that no one answer.

target_units.text: They kept silent and did not answer him a word, for the king had commanded, ‘Do not answer him.’

relationship: parallel report to Hezekiah by officials with torn clothing
rationale: Both bring the same three officials back to Hezekiah with torn garments to report the Assyrian spokesman's words. Isaiah additionally calls Somnas the army's scribe; the Kings verse names him simply as scribe.
source_text: Eliakim son of Chelkias, the steward, Somnas the army’s scribe, and Joach son of Asaph, the record-keeper, came to Hezekiah with torn tunics and reported Rapsakes’ words.

target_units.text: Eliakim son of Chelkias the steward, Somnas the scribe, and Joash son of Asaph the recorder came to Hezekiah with torn garments and reported Rhapsakes’s words to him.
